Probing the models' internal representations reveals that quiet features are learned prior to any decrease in task loss. These quiet features represent intermediate algorithmic computations that do not by themselves improve the output loss. Ablation experiments demonstrate that individual quiet features are causally necessary for task performance. Our results demonstrate that substantial representational progress can remain hidden beneath an apparently flat loss curve, challenging the prevailing use of cross-entropy as a proxy for learning and motivating richer diagnostics for monitoring model training.

papers.title: The Grammar-Learning Trajectories of Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: Do neural language models learn grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data? What does this consistency reveal about their inductive biases and linguistic representations?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models acquire grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data, indicating a shared inductive bias. The learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional, meaning that overall performance predicts which linguistic generalizations have been acquired.
papers.conclusion: Studying learning trajectories is a promising approach to understand linguistic representations in NLMs, and the consistency suggests a mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
NLMs with different random initializations learn grammatical phenomena in a highly correlated order.
Different architectures (GPT2 and TransformerXL) also show similar learning trajectories when aligned by performance level.
The choice of training data has some effect but does not override the consistent ordering.
The learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional: models with similar overall performance have similar performance on individual phenomena.
Early in training, NLMs rely on local cues and resemble bag-of-words models; later they become more sensitive to structural cues.
future_direction: Consider the impact of additional factors, architectures and learning phases that appear only later in training.
Develop a theory that can account for the patterns presented by NLMs’ learning trajectories.
papers.abstract: The learning trajectories of linguistic phenomena in humans provide insight into linguistic representation, beyond what can be gleaned from inspecting the behavior of an adult speaker. To apply a similar approach to analyze neural language models (NLM), it is first necessary to establish that different models are similar enough in the generalizations they make. In this paper, we show that NLMs with different initialization, architecture, and training data acquire linguistic phenomena in a similar order, despite their different end performance. These findings suggest that there is some mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena. Taking inspiration from psycholinguistics, we argue that studying this inductive bias is an opportunity to study the linguistic representation implicit in NLMs.

papers.title: Semantic and Structural Analysis of Implicit Biases in Large Language Models: An Interpretable Approach
papers.research_question: How to identify and explain implicit stereotypes in large language models using an interpretable bias detection method?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an interpretable bias detection method for large language models that integrates nested semantic representation with attention perturbation to identify hidden social biases in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The interpretable detection method effectively identifies implicit biases in LLMs, improving detection accuracy and semantic consistency, and provides a foundation for bias intervention and ethical deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves higher bias detection accuracy (84.7%), semantic consistency (91.2%), and lower contextual sensitivity (8.5) compared to baselines.
It demonstrates strong generalization across multiple stereotype dimensions, with higher accuracy for gender and profession than for religion and race.
Higher semantic similarity between texts leads to more consistent bias judgments, reducing conflict rates.
Attention perturbation analysis reveals the model's sensitivity to social attribute terms, helping uncover bias pathways.
The method provides interpretable insights into how implicit stereotypes are formed in language models.
papers.limitation: Performance declines on more complex, culturally embedded biases such as religion and race due to their subtlety and ambiguity.
future_direction: Expand the method's adaptability to cross-cultural and multilingual contexts.
Integrate external knowledge bases and user feedback signals for more flexible bias detection.
Embed interpretability mechanisms into model interaction interfaces for user perception and response.
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the issue of implicit stereotypes that may arise during the generation process of large language models. It proposes an interpretable bias detection method aimed at identifying hidden social biases in model outputs, especially those semantic tendencies that are not easily captured through explicit linguistic features. The method combines nested semantic representation with a contextual contrast mechanism. It extracts latent bias features from the vector space structure of model outputs. Using attention weight perturbation, it analyzes the model's sensitivity to specific social attribute terms, thereby revealing the semantic pathways through which bias is formed. To validate the effectiveness of the method, this study uses the StereoSet dataset, which covers multiple stereotype dimensions including gender, profession, religion, and race. The evaluation focuses on several key metrics, such as bias detection accuracy, semantic consistency, and contextual sensitivity. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves strong detection performance across various dimensions. It can accurately identify bias differences between semantically similar texts while maintaining high semantic alignment and output stability. The method also demonstrates high interpretability in its structural design. It helps uncover the internal bias association mechanisms within language models. This provides a more transparent and reliable technical foundation for bias detection. The approach is suitable for real-world applications where high trustworthiness of generated content is required.

papers.title: Unrewarded Exploration in Large Language Models Reveals Latent Learning from Psychology
papers.abstract: Latent learning, classically theorized by Tolman, shows that biological agents (e.g., rats) can acquire internal representations of their environment without rewards, enabling rapid adaptation once rewards are introduced. In contrast, from a cognitive science perspective, reward learning remains overly dependent on external feedback, limiting flexibility and generalization. Although recent advances in the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), such as OpenAI-o1 and DeepSeek-R1, mark a significant breakthrough, these models still rely primarily on reward-centric reinforcement learning paradigms. Whether and how the well-established phenomenon of latent learning in psychology can inform or emerge within LLMs' training remains largely unexplored. In this work, we present novel findings from our experiments that LLMs also exhibit the latent learning dynamics. During an initial phase of unrewarded exploration, LLMs display modest performance improvements, as this phase allows LLMs to organize task-relevant knowledge without being constrained by reward-driven biases, and performance is further enhanced once rewards are introduced. LLMs post-trained under this two-stage exploration regime ultimately achieve higher competence than those post-trained with reward-based reinforcement learning throughout. Beyond these empirical observations, we also provide theoretical analyses for our experiments explaining why unrewarded exploration yields performance gains, offering a mechanistic account of these dynamics. Specifically, we conducted extensive experiments across multiple model families and diverse task domains to establish the existence of the latent learning dynamics in LLMs.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: Linear socio-demographic representations emerge in Large Language Models from indirect cues
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode sociodemographic attributes of human conversational partners inferred from indirect cues such as names and occupations, and do these representations shape downstream behavior?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs develop linear representations of user sociodemographic attributes within their activation space from indirect cues, and these representations actively shape downstream behavior, revealing an alignment gap where models refuse explicit demographic queries but act on implicit biases.
papers.conclusion: LLMs linearly encode user demographic attributes from indirect cues, and these representations have measurable behavioral consequences, posing significant challenges for fairness in deployed conversational AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode user sociodemographics in linear subspaces of activation space that can be decoded with high accuracy using linear probes.
Implicit cues such as names and occupations trigger demographic representations aligned with real-world population statistics (e.g., US Census, Bureau of Labor Statistics).
Inference-time interventions (activation steering) demonstrate that these linear representations causally influence model outputs, such as country-of-origin or name predictions.
Models exhibit an alignment gap: commercial models refuse explicit demographic-based reasoning while implicitly encoding and acting upon demographics inferred from contextual cues.
Stereotypical associations in the model's representations correlate with distributional patterns in the training data, as shown for OLMo and Common Crawl.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic prompts designed for experimental control; generalization to organic user interactions is uncertain.
Binary demographic categories (male/female, Black/White, rich/poor) fail to capture the continuous and multidimensional nature of human identity.
The prompts and data sources (US Census, BLS, Kozlowski et al. survey) reflect Western and primarily American cultural framings.
The findings demonstrate correlational patterns between training data, representations, and behavior but do not establish causation.
future_direction: Deeper cross-cultural analysis to understand how biases manifest across different cultural contexts.
Establishing causal relationships between training data, internal representations, and behavioral outputs.
Developing and evaluating intervention techniques (e.g., activation steering, representation debiasing) to mitigate bias without compromising model capabilities.
papers.abstract: We investigate how LLMs encode sociodemographic attributes of human conversational partners inferred from indirect cues such as names and occupations. We show that LLMs develop linear representations of user demographics within activation space, wherein stereotypically associated attributes are encoded along interpretable geometric directions. We first probe residual streams across layers of four open transformer-based LLMs (Magistral 24B, Qwen3 14B, GPT-OSS 20B, OLMo2-1B) prompted with explicit demographic disclosure. We show that the same probes predict demographics from implicit cues: names activate census-aligned gender and race representations, while occupations trigger representations correlated with real-world workforce statistics. These linear representations allow us to explain demographic inferences implicitly formed by LLMs during conversation. We demonstrate that these implicit demographic representations actively shape downstream behavior, such as career recommendations. Our study further highlights that models that pass bias benchmark tests may still harbor and leverage implicit biases, with implications for fairness when applied at scale.

papers.title: Enhancing Multiple Dimensions of Trustworthiness in LLMs via Sparse Activation Control
papers.research_question: How can we enhance multiple dimensions of trustworthiness (safety, factuality, bias) in LLMs simultaneously without training, by controlling sparse activations in specific model components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Control, a training-free method that enhances multiple trustworthiness dimensions in LLMs by identifying sparse, task-specific attention heads and controlling their representations using Gaussian Mixture Models, avoiding control conflicts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Activation Control is an effective training-free method for enhancing multi-dimensional trustworthiness in LLMs by leveraging sparse and independent task-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Activation Control can enhance safety, factuality, and bias simultaneously without significant interference, outperforming representation engineering baselines in multi-task control.
Attention heads for different tasks are sparse and have minimal overlap, allowing independent control.
The method does not significantly harm general model performance on MMLU and CSQA.
The method generalizes to other models (Qwen series) and additional trustworthiness tasks (robustness, privacy).
Control shifts head outputs towards task-relevant tokens, as shown by unembedding projections.
papers.limitation:
Relies on construction of paired stimuli, which may require domain knowledge.
Experiments are limited to a few models and tasks.
future_direction: Extend to more tasks and models
Explore theoretical foundations of sparsity
papers.abstract: As the development and application of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance rapidly, enhancing their trustworthiness and aligning them with human preferences has become a critical area of research. Traditional methods rely heavily on extensive data for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), but representation engineering offers a new, training-free approach. This technique leverages semantic features to control the representation of LLM's intermediate hidden states, enabling the model to meet specific requirements such as increased honesty or heightened safety awareness. However, a significant challenge arises when attempting to fulfill multiple requirements simultaneously. It proves difficult to encode various semantic contents, like honesty and safety, into a singular semantic feature, restricting its practicality. In this work, we address this issue through ``Sparse Activation Control''. By delving into the intrinsic mechanisms of LLMs, we manage to identify and pinpoint components that are closely related to specific tasks within the model, i.e., attention heads. These heads display sparse characteristics that allow for near-independent control over different tasks. Our experiments, conducted on the open-source Llama series models, have yielded encouraging results. The models were able to align with human preferences on issues of safety, factuality, and bias concurrently.

papers.title: Curved Inference: A Guide to Geometric Interpretability
papers.research_question: How do token representations evolve geometrically in the residual stream of transformer-based language models, and how does this geometry relate to semantic structure and complex behaviors like concern, deception, and self-modeling?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Curved Inference framework, a geometric approach to interpretability that measures how token representations evolve in the residual stream, demonstrating that these trajectories reflect semantic structure and are associated with behaviors like concern, deception, and self-modeling.
papers.conclusion: Curved Inference provides a geometric framework for interpretability that shifts focus from static attribution to dynamic inference analysis, offering a model-faithful lens to understand internal computation in transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream trajectories are semantically sensitive and show structured curvature in response to concern-shifted prompts.
Residual geometry diverges in cases of latent behavioral shifts, such as deception in sleeper agents, and can precede output changes.
Curvature is functionally associated with sustained self-modeling, persisting even under curvature-penalizing fine-tuning.
Geometric metrics like curvature, salience, and semantic surface area provide reproducible signals across multiple domains.
The residual stream is the exclusive locus for this geometric signal, unlike attention or MLP outputs.
papers.limitation:
Geometric derivatives rely on interpolation assumptions that may not hold in all cases.
Dependence on external LLM classifiers for alignment and intent judgments introduces biases.
Experiments were conducted on models up to 3b parameters, so results may not generalize to larger or opaque systems.
future_direction: Scale testing with larger models
Extending analysis to tasks involving reasoning, planning, or complex dialogue
Formalizing curvature signatures for specific generative behaviors
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a unified framework for analyzing the internal geometry of inference in transformer-based language models. Building on a series of prior studies, we present a consolidated introduction to “Curved Inference”: a methodology that measures how token representations evolve in the residual stream as geometric trajectories. Using metrics such as curvature, salience, and semantic surface area, we show that residual trajectories reflect meaningful semantic structure, and are empirically associated with emotional and moral concern, covert intent in sleeper agents, and computational self-modeling dynamics. We consolidate these findings into a reproducible, falsifiable pipeline, supported by formal mathematical definitions and open-source tools. This geometric approach shifts the focus of interpretability from static attribution to dynamic, modelnative inference analysis. The results provide evidence that residual stream geometry is not only measurable, but also structurally related to complex behaviors in the models we study. We invite researchers to replicate, extend, or falsify these claims and test the boundaries of curved inference as a new paradigm for model understanding. Received: 6 August 2025 | Revised: 12 January 2026 | Accepted: 21 January 2026 Conflicts of Interest The author declares that he has no conflicts of interest to this work. Data Availability Statement The data that support the findings of this study are openly available in GitHub at https://github.com/robman/FRESH-model/tree/main/ benchmarks/curved-inference. Author Contribution Statement Rob Manson: Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Validation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Resources, Data curation, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing, Visualization, Supervision, Project administration.

papers.title: Decoding Emotion in the Deep: A Systematic Study of How LLMs Represent, Retain, and Express Emotion
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to navigate the nuances of human emotion. While research confirms that LLMs can simulate emotional intelligence, their internal emotional mechanisms remain largely unexplored. This paper investigates the latent emotional representations within modern LLMs by asking: how, where, and for how long is emotion encoded in their neural architecture? To address this, we introduce a novel, large-scale Reddit corpus of approximately 400,000 utterances, balanced across seven basic emotions through a multi-stage process of classification, rewriting, and synthetic generation. Using this dataset, we employ lightweight "probes" to read out information from the hidden layers of various Qwen3 and LLaMA models without altering their parameters. Our findings reveal that LLMs develop a surprisingly well-defined internal geometry of emotion, which sharpens with model scale and significantly outperforms zero-shot prompting. We demonstrate that this emotional signal is not a final-layer phenomenon but emerges early and peaks mid-network. Furthermore, the internal states are both malleable (they can be influenced by simple system prompts) and persistent, as the initial emotional tone remains detectable for hundreds of subsequent tokens. We contribute our dataset, an open-source probing toolkit, and a detailed map of the emotional landscape within LLMs, offering crucial insights for developing more transparent and aligned AI systems. The code and dataset are open-sourced.

papers.title: Gender Encoding Patterns in Pretrained Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How do pretrained language models internally represent and propagate gender biases? How do bias mitigation techniques and fine-tuning affect these encoded biases?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a consistent pattern of gender encoding in pretrained language models (early layers suppress, later layers amplify) and shows that debiasing techniques, especially post-hoc methods, are limited in altering internal representations, while fine-tuning reduces encoded gender information but may concentrate bias in the classification layer.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that gender bias is deeply embedded in pretrained language models and that current debiasing techniques are insufficient, advocating for proactive integration of fairness objectives during pretraining and targeted interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Gender information follows a consistent encoding pattern across encoder models: early layers suppress gender signals, while later layers amplify them.
Debiasing techniques, especially post-hoc methods, show limited efficacy in reducing encoded gender bias in internal representations.
Training-time Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA) is the most effective debiasing method for reducing gender encoding.
Fine-tuning on a downstream task (occupation classification) reduces gender information in the encoder representations, but may concentrate bias in the classification layer.
Larger models (e.g., BERT-large) tend to encode more gender information than smaller models.
papers.limitation:
Focus on gender bias in English-language biographies, leaving broader sociocultural and intersectional biases unexplored.
The study centers on encoder-based models; future work should validate findings in decoder-based architectures and multimodal systems.
The interplay between task-specific fine-tuning and bias propagation requires deeper exploration across diverse applications.
future_direction: Extend analysis to broader sociocultural and intersectional biases.
Validate findings in decoder-based architectures and multimodal systems.
Explore the interplay between fine-tuning and bias propagation across diverse applications.
papers.abstract: Gender bias in pretrained language models (PLMs) poses significant social and ethical challenges.Despite growing awareness, there is a lack of comprehensive investigation into how different models internally represent and propagate such biases.This study adopts an information-theoretic approach to analyze how gender biases are encoded within various encoder-based architectures.We focus on three key aspects: identifying how models encode gender information and biases, examining the impact of bias mitigation techniques and fine-tuning on the encoded biases and their effectiveness, and exploring how model design differences influence the encoding of biases.Through rigorous and systematic investigation, our findings reveal a consistent pattern of gender encoding across diverse models.Surprisingly, debiasing techniques often exhibit limited efficacy, sometimes inadvertently increasing the encoded bias in internal representations while reducing bias in model output distributions.This highlights a disconnect between mitigating bias in output distributions and addressing its internal representations.This work provides valuable guidance for advancing bias mitigation strategies and fostering the development of more equitable language models. 1

papers.title: How Does Controllability Emerge In Language Models During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How does linear steerability emerge in language models during pretraining, and why does it vary across concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Linear steerability emerges during intermediate stages of training, varies across concepts, and is linked to increasing linear separability of concepts in the hidden space.
papers.conclusion: Linear steerability does not emerge uniformly but develops over training and varies between concepts, aligning with increasingly structured internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Linear steerability emerges in later training stages, separate from reasoning capability and emotion expression via prompting.
Emergence times vary widely across concepts, such as anger emerging earlier than sadness.
Concept representations become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses.
The Intervention Detector (ID) framework can reveal steerability dynamics and predict when linear steerability emerges.
These findings hold across different model families, indicating a general pattern.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated on 7B-scale open-source models, not tested on larger LLMs.
Intervention coefficient was empirically tuned and differs across models, with underlying causes not investigated.
Did not explore alternative nonlinear approaches for extracting or intervening in model representations.
Methodological innovation in intervention techniques is not the focus; core procedure is consistent with prior work.
Alternative unsupervised methods such as mean-difference vectors are not compared.
Concepts like emotions lack ground truth, making evaluation subjective and based on semantic interpretation.
Steering certain concepts can produce offensive outputs, with no safety filtering applied.
future_direction: Examining how different pre-training corpora influence intervention outcomes.
Exploring alternative steering methods beyond PCA or K-Means.
Comparing unsupervised methods like mean-difference vectors and their influence on downstream intervention performance.
papers.abstract: Language models can be steered by modifying their internal representations to control concepts such as emotion, style, or truthfulness in generation. However, the conditions for an effective intervention remain unclear and are often validated through heuristics and trial-and-error. To fill this gap, we demonstrate that intervention efficacy, measured by linear steerability (i.e., the ability to adjust output via linear transformations of hidden states), emerges during intermediate stages of training. Moreover, even closely related concepts (e.g., anger and sadness) exhibit steerability emergence at distinct stages of training. To better interpret the dynamics of steerability during training, we adapt existing intervention techniques into a unified framework, referred to as the "Intervention Detector" (ID), which is designed to reveal how linear steerability evolves over the course of training through hidden state and representation analysis. ID reveals that concepts become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses, which strongly correlates with the emergence of linear steerability. We further introduce ID-based metrics, such as heatmaps, entropy trends, and cosine similarity, to help interpret how linear steerability evolves throughout training. In addition, we apply ID across different model families to ensure the generality of our findings on steerability dynamics.

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Language Models Are Specific to Human Language
papers.research_question: Are correlations between language model hidden states and fMRI brain responses robust to dimensionality concerns, and are they specific to models trained on human language and dependent on positional encoding?
papers.core_contribution: The study confirms that correlations between transformer language model hidden states and human brain activity during language tasks are robust, specific to language-trained models, and heavily dependent on positional encodings.
papers.conclusion: The internal representations of transformer language models are strongly correlated with human brain activity during language processing, and this alignment is specific to language-trained models and relies on positional information.
papers.key_findings:
Removing positional encodings significantly reduces brain-model correlations and distorts the geometric similarity between model and brain representational spaces.
Dimensionality reduction via PCA does not eliminate the correlations, indicating they are not an artifact of the curse of dimensionality.
Models trained on non-linguistic data (protein sequences) show negligible alignment with brain activity, confirming the language-specificity of the effects.
Causal (decoder-only) language models show higher alignment with brain activity than bidirectional models.
The geometric structure of model and brain representations, measured by CKA and Gromov-Wasserstein distance, is similar and degrades when positional information is removed.
papers.limitation:
The dataset includes only 243 stimuli and 6 subjects, limiting statistical power and generalizability.
The head-wise analysis pooled voxels across cortical regions without distinguishing between different regions of interest.
The study uses text-only models and fMRI data from reading tasks; future work should use modality-matched datasets (e.g., audio models with spoken language tasks).
future_direction: Increase the number of subjects and model diversity to improve statistical power and generalizability.
Conduct finer-grained region-of-interest (ROI) by head analysis to reveal differential alignment patterns.
Use modality-matched datasets (e.g., spoken-language tasks with audio models) to disentangle task effects from representational differences.
papers.abstract: Previous work has shown correlations between the hidden states of large language models and fMRI brain responses, on language tasks. These correlations have been taken as evidence of the representational similarity of these models and brain states. This study tests whether these previous results are robust to several possible concerns. Specifically this study shows: (i) that the previous results are still found after dimensionality reduction, and thus are not attributable to the curse of dimensionality; (ii) that previous results are confirmed when using new measures of similarity; (iii) that correlations between brain representations and those from models are specific to models trained on human language; and (iv) that the results are dependent on the presence of positional encoding in the models. These results confirm and strengthen the results of previous research and contribute to the debate on the biological plausibility and interpretability of state-of-the-art large language models.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Psychological Simulators: A Methodological Guide
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a methodological framework and guidelines for using LLMs as psychological simulators in two primary applications: simulating roles/personas and serving as cognitive models, while addressing challenges and ethical considerations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs are tools to augment, not replace, human-centered research, and their effective use requires precision, rigor, and a dual commitment from psychologists and the AI community.
papers.limitation:
LLMs have temporal limitations due to training data cutoffs, preventing them from reflecting events, cultural shifts, or emerging knowledge after the cutoff date.
LLMs exhibit cultural and demographic biases due to overrepresentation of WEIRD populations in training data, which can distort simulations of marginalized groups or non-Western cultures.
LLMs often fail to capture the full range of human psychological diversity, showing more extreme and less nuanced preference distributions compared to human participants.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer emerging opportunities for psychological and behavioral research, but methodological guidance is lacking. This article provides a framework for using LLMs as psychological simulators across two primary applications: simulating roles and personas to explore diverse contexts, and serving as computational models to investigate cognitive processes. For simulation, we present methods for developing psychologically grounded personas that move beyond demographic categories, with strategies for validation against human data and use cases ranging from studying inaccessible populations to prototyping research instruments. For cognitive modeling, we synthesize emerging approaches for probing internal representations, methodological advances in causal interventions, and strategies for relating model behavior to human cognition. We address overarching challenges including prompt sensitivity, temporal limitations from training data cutoffs, and ethical considerations that extend beyond traditional human subjects review. Throughout, we emphasize the need for transparency about model capabilities and constraints. Together, this framework integrates emerging empirical evidence about LLM performance--including systematic biases, cultural limitations, and prompt brittleness--to help researchers wrangle these challenges and leverage the unique capabilities of LLMs in psychological research.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task
papers.research_question: Does a sequence model trained on a synthetic task (Othello game transcripts) learn an internal representation of the board state, and is that representation causal to its predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that a GPT model trained on Othello game transcripts learns a nonlinear internal representation of the board state, which is causally involved in its predictions. It introduces intervention techniques and latent saliency maps for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide evidence that Othello-GPT maintains a nonlinear internal representation of the game board state, which is causally linked to its predictions. The tools introduced (nonlinear probes, interventions, latent saliency maps) may prove useful for interpretability in natural language settings.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT predicts legal moves with high accuracy, and this is not due to memorization.
Nonlinear probes can accurately decode the board state from internal activations, while linear probes perform poorly.
Intervention experiments show that the board representation is causal to the model's predictions.
Latent saliency maps reveal differences between models trained on synthetic vs. championship data, indicating different learned strategies.
The internal representation of the board state is nonlinear and emerges during training.
papers.limitation: Latent saliency maps only attribute to one tile when multiple tiles are involved in a move, which does not fully capture the Othello rule logic.
future_direction: Extend investigation to other, more complex games.
Compare strategies learned by a sequence model with those of a model trained with a priori knowledge of Othello.
Study how results generalize to natural language models.
papers.abstract: Language models show a surprising range of capabilities, but the source of their apparent competence is unclear. Do these networks just memorize a collection of surface statistics, or do they rely on internal representations of the process that generates the sequences they see? We investigate this question by applying a variant of the GPT model to the task of predicting legal moves in a simple board game, Othello. Although the network has no a priori knowledge of the game or its rules, we uncover evidence of an emergent nonlinear internal representation of the board state. Interventional experiments indicate this representation can be used to control the output of the network and create "latent saliency maps" that can help explain predictions in human terms.

papers.title: Monolingual and Multilingual Reduction of Gender Bias in Contextualized Representations
papers.research_question: How can we effectively reduce gender bias in contextualized representations using DensRay, and how is gender information distributed in BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using DensRay to debias contextualized representations, showing it performs comparably to prior methods, is more robust, preserves language model performance better, and enables multilingual debiasing.
papers.conclusion: DensRay is an effective method for reducing gender bias in contextualized representations, maintaining model performance, and can be applied multilingually.
papers.key_findings:
DensRay effectively mitigates gender bias on OCCTMP and association tests.
DensRay preserves language model performance on Wikitext-2 and GLUE tasks better than other methods.
Gender information is spread across all attention heads and most layers in BERT, with no single head responsible.
DensRay can obtain gender bias scores on token and sentence levels.
DensRay can be used for zero-shot multilingual debiasing (e.g., debias Chinese using English data).
papers.limitation:
Token-level bias scores work well for monolingual BERT but not for multilingual BERT.
The method focuses only on the gender direction and may not address biases from implicitly gendered terms.
future_direction: Investigate multilingual transfer of debiasing techniques more closely.
Investigate debiasing with non-binary approaches (beyond male-female binary).
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (PLMs) learn stereotypes held by humans and reflected in text from their training corpora, including gender bias. When PLMs are used for downstream tasks such as picking candidates for a job, people's lives can be negatively affected by these learned stereotypes. Prior work usually identifies a linear gender subspace and removes gender information by eliminating the subspace. Following this line of work, we propose to use DensRay, an analytical method for obtaining interpretable dense subspaces. We show that DensRay performs on-par with prior approaches, but provide arguments that it is more robust and provide indications that it preserves language model performance better. By applying DensRay to attention heads and layers of BERT we show that gender information is spread across all attention heads and most of the layers. Also we show that DensRay can obtain gender bias scores on both token and sentence levels. Finally, we demonstrate that we can remove bias multilingually, e.g., from Chinese, using only English training data.

papers.title: Unveiling Theory of Mind in Large Language Models: A Parallel to Single Neurons in the Human Brain
papers.research_question: What are the similarities between LLMs' hidden embeddings and human neurons in representing Theory of Mind, specifically in responding to true- and false-belief trials?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs exhibit hidden embeddings that selectively respond to Theory of Mind tasks, showing parallels to human neuronal activity in the dorsal medial prefrontal cortex.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals emergent ToM-related embeddings in LLMs, indicating a parallel between artificial models and human brain neurons in encoding Theory of Mind information.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform better on true-belief trials than false-belief trials, with larger models showing higher accuracy.
Hidden embeddings in LLMs show significant differences in activity between true- and false-belief trials, similar to human neurons.
The percentage of responsive embeddings increases with model size and correlates with ToM performance.
Trial types (true vs false belief) can be decoded from population embeddings with high accuracy, especially in larger models.
Control experiments confirm that these effects depend on contextual information in the statements.
papers.limitation:
Limited to open-source LLMs without access to higher-performing models like GPT-4.
Methods focused only on embeddings selective to one trial type, excluding those selective to both.
papers.abstract: With their recent development, large language models (LLMs) have been found to exhibit a certain level of Theory of Mind (ToM), a complex cognitive capacity that is related to our conscious mind and that allows us to infer another's beliefs and perspective. While human ToM capabilities are believed to derive from the neural activity of a broadly interconnected brain network, including that of dorsal medial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) neurons, the precise processes underlying LLM's capacity for ToM or their similarities with that of humans remains largely unknown. In this study, we drew inspiration from the dmPFC neurons subserving human ToM and employed a similar methodology to examine whether LLMs exhibit comparable characteristics. Surprisingly, our analysis revealed a striking resemblance between the two, as hidden embeddings (artificial neurons) within LLMs started to exhibit significant responsiveness to either true- or false-belief trials, suggesting their ability to represent another's perspective. These artificial embedding responses were closely correlated with the LLMs' performance during the ToM tasks, a property that was dependent on the size of the models. Further, the other's beliefs could be accurately decoded using the entire embeddings, indicating the presence of the embeddings' ToM capability at the population level. Together, our findings revealed an emergent property of LLMs' embeddings that modified their activities in response to ToM features, offering initial evidence of a parallel between the artificial model and neurons in the human brain.

papers.title: Personas as a Way to Model Truthfulness in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models distinguish truth from falsehood in a noisy dataset? The paper presents an explanation for why LMs appear to know the truth despite not being trained with truth labels.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the persona hypothesis: that language models learn to distinguish truth from falsehood by inferring and representing truthful personas from the pretraining data, which are clusters of agents with common features.
papers.conclusion: The persona hypothesis explains how LLMs model truthfulness by inferring personas from agent clusters in pretraining data, supported by evidence from LLM probing and synthetic experiments.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can predict answer truthfulness from question embeddings, indicating that models infer persona from context.
Finetuning on truthful QA pairs generalizes to unseen topics, suggesting a global truthful persona representation.
In synthetic settings, models distinguish truth only when training data has a truthful persona (clustered agents).
Models encode both truthful and untruthful answers and select based on persona, implying a selection mechanism.
papers.limitation:
Probe accuracy is only about 70%, indicating models do not perfectly learn truthfulness.
The latent features used for clustering may be spurious, not robust truthfulness.
Synthetic setting uses explicit agent tokens and assumes equal complexity and shared beliefs, which may not hold in real data.
future_direction: Investigate the persona-based computation mechanism on larger models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on vast amounts of text from the internet, which contains both factual and misleading information about the world. While unintuitive from a classic view of LMs, recent work has shown that the truth value of a statement can be elicited from the model's representations. This paper presents an explanation for why LMs appear to know the truth despite not being trained with truth labels. We hypothesize that the pretraining data is generated by groups of (un)truthful agents whose outputs share common features, and they form a (un)truthful persona. By training on this data, LMs can infer and represent the persona in its activation space. This allows the model to separate truth from falsehoods and controls the truthfulness of its generation. We show evidence for the persona hypothesis via two observations: (1) we can probe whether a model's answer will be truthful before it is generated; (2) finetuning a model on a set of facts improves its truthfulness on unseen topics. Next, using arithmetics as a synthetic environment, we show that structures of the pretraining data are crucial for the model to infer the truthful persona. Overall, our findings suggest that models can exploit hierarchical structures in the data to learn abstract concepts like truthfulness.

papers.title: Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
papers.research_question: How can causal mediation analysis be used to interpret the internal mechanisms of neural NLP models, specifically to understand the role of individual components (like neurons and attention heads) in mediating gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a structural-behavioral framework based on causal mediation analysis for interpreting neural NLP models, and applies it to gender bias, revealing that bias effects are sparse, synergistic, and decomposable into direct and indirect effects.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis provides a useful framework for interpreting neural NLP models, offering insights into the internal mechanisms by which properties like gender bias flow from input to output through various model components.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias effects are sparse, concentrated in a relatively small number of model components (neurons and attention heads).
Gender bias effects are synergistic, with different model components interacting to amplify or repress their individual effects.
Gender bias effects are decomposable, with the total effect approximating the sum of direct and indirect effects, despite model non-linearity.
Larger models tend to exhibit larger gender bias effects.
The causal mediation analysis framework captures general patterns of causal structure in Transformer architectures, not just model-specific characteristics.
papers.limitation:
The experimental design focuses on gender bias in a binary setup, which does not account for a gender-inclusive spectrum.
Preliminary experiments with gender-neutral references (e.g., singular 'they') showed models have not learned these concepts well, and the setup suffers from confounders like plural 'they'.
Results for masked language models (e.g., BERT) are less clear, potentially due to differences in scoring multi-token continuations compared to autoregressive models.
future_direction: Applying the methodology to more gender-inclusive setups and other kinds of biases.
Using mediation analysis to guide the development of new debiasing methods that establish counterfactual fairness.
Exploring path-specific effects to identify exact mechanisms through which biases arise.
papers.abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.

papers.title: Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language
papers.research_question: Do large language models have the ability to introspect about their internal linguistic knowledge, specifically grammatical knowledge and word prediction?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs do not exhibit introspection about their linguistic knowledge; their metalinguistic responses are not more aligned with their own internal probabilities than with those of similar models.
papers.conclusion: LLMs cannot introspect about their linguistic knowledge, and metalinguistic prompting should not be conflated with models' internal linguistic generalizations.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve high accuracy on grammaticality and word prediction tasks under both direct (probability-based) and metalinguistic (prompt-based) evaluation methods.
The consistency between direct and metalinguistic evaluations is low (Cohen’s κ around 0.25).
There is no evidence of introspection: within-model alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations is not higher than cross-model alignment when controlling for model similarity.
Model similarity (both feature-based and empirical) predicts the alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations, but there is no additional 'same model effect'.
Larger models tend to have better performance on metalinguistic prompts and their metalinguistic responses are more correlated with direct evaluations.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested open-source models; closed-source models might behave differently.
The null result might be due to the specific tasks and models; introspection might emerge in other settings.
papers.abstract: There has been recent interest in whether large language models (LLMs) can introspect about their own internal states. Such abilities would make LLMs more interpretable, and also validate the use of standard introspective methods in linguistics to evaluate grammatical knowledge in models (e.g., asking "Is this sentence grammatical?"). We systematically investigate emergent introspection across 21 open-source LLMs, in two domains where introspection is of theoretical interest: grammatical knowledge and word prediction. Crucially, in both domains, a model's internal linguistic knowledge can be theoretically grounded in direct measurements of string probability. We then evaluate whether models' responses to metalinguistic prompts faithfully reflect their internal knowledge. We propose a new measure of introspection: the degree to which a model's prompted responses predict its own string probabilities, beyond what would be predicted by another model with nearly identical internal knowledge. While both metalinguistic prompting and probability comparisons lead to high task accuracy, we do not find evidence that LLMs have privileged "self-access". By using general tasks, controlling for model similarity, and evaluating a wide range of open-source models, we show that LLMs cannot introspect, and add new evidence to the argument that prompted responses should not be conflated with models' linguistic generalizations.

papers.title: Why Representation Engineering Works: A Theoretical and Empirical Study in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Representation Engineering (RepE) be extended to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and what theoretical principles explain the stability of neural activity across layers in this context?
papers.core_contribution: This work extends Representation Engineering (RepE) to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and provides a theoretical framework explaining that the stability of neural activity across layers is governed by the principal eigenvector of the attention matrix, while a shrinking spectral gap allows subdominant eigenvectors to differentiate between concepts.
papers.conclusion: By integrating theoretical analysis with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new avenues for improving AI robustness, interpretability, and transparency in multimodal settings.
papers.key_findings:
The principal eigenvector of the self-attention matrix serves as a stable 'backbone' for neural activity propagation across layers.
The spectral gap (difference between the largest and second-largest eigenvalues) shrinks in deeper layers, enabling subdominant eigenvectors to capture subtle distinctions between concepts like honesty and fairness.
Representation Engineering (RepE) is effective in VLMs for extracting and analyzing high-level conceptual representations, such as honesty and fairness, from internal activations.
Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) scans reveal distinct activation patterns across layers for different high-level concepts, demonstrating how representations evolve through the network.
future_direction: Extend RepE to broader multimodal settings, exploring its potential for bias mitigation, honest detection, and countless concept applications.
papers.abstract: Representation Engineering (RepE) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing AI transparency by focusing on high-level representations rather than individual neurons or circuits. It has proven effective in improving interpretability and control, showing that representations can emerge, propagate, and shape final model outputs in large language models (LLMs). However, in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), visual input can override factual linguistic knowledge, leading to hallucinated responses that contradict reality. To address this challenge, we make the first attempt to extend RepE to VLMs, analyzing how multimodal representations are preserved and transformed. Building on our findings and drawing inspiration from successful RepE applications, we develop a theoretical framework that explains the stability of neural activity across layers using the principal eigenvector, uncovering the underlying mechanism of RepE. We empirically validate these instrinsic properties, demonstrating their broad applicability and significance. By bridging theoretical insights with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new directions for improving AI robustness, fairness, and transparency.

papers.title: Analysing Moral Bias in Finetuned LLMs through Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LLMs exhibit the Knobe effect (a moral bias in intentionality judgments), whether specific Transformer layers encode this bias, and whether targeted interventions (layer-patching) can mitigate it.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the Knobe effect (a moral bias) emerges in finetuned LLMs, is localized in mid-to-late Transformer layers, and can be mitigated by patching activations from pretrained models into finetuned models, without retraining.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that social biases in LLMs can be mechanistically localized and mitigated through targeted interventions like layer-patching, offering a method for model repair without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Finetuned LLMs exhibit the Knobe effect (moral bias in intentionality judgments), while pretrained models show minimal effect.
The bias is localized in mid-to-late Transformer layers, as shown by differences in residual stream activations.
Patching activations from pretrained models into specific layers of finetuned models can reduce or eliminate the bias.
The mitigation via layer-patching does not significantly harm general model performance on standard benchmarks.
The Knobe effect is not an emergent property of model scale alone; it is induced by finetuning and appears across model sizes.
papers.limitation: The layer-patching method requires access to the pretrained model.
future_direction: Explore whether this localization technique applies to other biases, such as gender or racial stereotypes.
Develop methods that do not rely on access to the pretrained model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to internalize human-like biases during finetuning, yet the mechanisms by which these biases manifest remain unclear. In this work, we investigated whether the well-known Knobe effect, a moral bias in intentionality judgements, emerges in finetuned LLMs and whether it can be traced back to specific components of the model. We conducted a Layer-Patching analysis across 3 open-weights LLMs and demonstrated that the bias is not only learned during finetuning but also localized in a specific set of layers. Surprisingly, we found that patching activations from the corresponding pretrained model into just a few critical layers is sufficient to eliminate the effect. Our findings offer new evidence that social biases in LLMs can be interpreted, localized, and mitigated through targeted interventions, without the need for model retraining.

papers.title: Interpreting Gender Bias in Neural Machine Translation: Multilingual Architecture Matters
papers.research_question: Does the multilingual neural machine translation architecture impact the degree of gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language-specific encoder-decoders exhibit less gender bias than shared architectures, and proposes two interpretability methods based on source embeddings and attention to explain this difference.
papers.conclusion: The choice of multilingual architecture impacts gender bias in machine translation, and the proposed interpretability methods help explain why language-specific models perform better by showing they encode more gender information and have more diverted attention.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific encoder-decoders show less gender bias than shared encoder-decoders when trained on the same data.
Language-specific models encode more gender information in source embeddings, as measured by SVM classification accuracy.
Language-specific models have more diverted attention, allowing them to consider a broader context when predicting gender.
Bilingual systems vary in the amount of gender information encoded in embeddings depending on the target language.
Most gender translation errors involve assuming masculine occupations, which may be due to data imbalances and linguistic/cultural factors.
papers.limitation: The conclusions are based on the WinoMT benchmark, which has known downsides such as unnaturalness and logical failures, potentially affecting the results.
future_direction: Providing real-world data benchmarks to evaluate gender accuracy in machine translation systems.
Experimenting with more distant language pairs to see if the conclusions hold.
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation architectures mainly differ in the number of sharing modules and parameters applied among languages. In this paper, and from an algorithmic perspective, we explore whether the chosen architecture, when trained with the same data, influences the level of gender bias. Experiments conducted in three language pairs show that language-specific encoder-decoders exhibit less bias than the shared architecture. We propose two methods for interpreting and studying gender bias in machine translation based on source embeddings and attention. Our analysis shows that, in the language-specific case, the embeddings encode more gender information, and their attention is more diverted. Both behaviors help in mitigating gender bias.

papers.title: On the Pitfalls of Analyzing Individual Neurons in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the pitfalls in the common methodology for ranking individual neurons in language models, and how can we better evaluate neuron rankings by separating probe quality from ranking quality and focusing on information used by the model?
papers.core_contribution: This paper identifies two pitfalls in neuron ranking methods (conflating probe and ranking quality, and focusing on encoded rather than used information), and introduces a probe-less ranking method (PROBELESS) that better identifies neurons actually used by the model.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the importance of separating probe quality from ranking quality and of evaluating rankings based on information used by the model, introducing a probe-less ranking method that is effective for identifying causally relevant neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Probe quality and ranking quality are confounded; a good probe can yield high accuracy even with a bad ranking, masking the ranking's true quality.
Encoded information is not the same as information used by the model; a ranking good for probing may not select neurons that are causally important for the model's output.
The proposed PROBELESS ranking, based on simple data statistics, tends to select neurons that are more used by the model than rankings from probe-based methods (LINEAR and GAUSSIAN).
The GAUSSIAN probe often achieves high accuracy by memorizing word-type–label pairs, leading to low selectivity, whereas LINEAR is more stable and selective.
There is an overlap between encoded and used information, but they are not identical, highlighting the need to evaluate rankings based on used information via interventions.
papers.abstract: While many studies have shown that linguistic information is encoded in hidden word representations, few have studied individual neurons, to show how and in which neurons it is encoded. Among these, the common approach is to use an external probe to rank neurons according to their relevance to some linguistic attribute, and to evaluate the obtained ranking using the same probe that produced it. We show two pitfalls in this methodology: 1. It confounds distinct factors: probe quality and ranking quality. We separate them and draw conclusions on each. 2. It focuses on encoded information, rather than information that is used by the model. We show that these are not the same. We compare two recent ranking methods and a simple one we introduce, and evaluate them with regard to both of these aspects.

papers.title: Emergence of Linear Truth Encodings in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why and how do linear truth subspaces that separate true from false statements emerge in language models during training and inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the statistical co-occurrence of true/false statements (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis), demonstrated through a toy transformer model and experiments.
papers.conclusion: Linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the co-occurrence statistics of true and false statements, as demonstrated by a toy model and supported by experiments in pretrained models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear truth encoding emerges in a one-layer transformer trained on data where true/false statements co-occur (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis).
Training exhibits two phases: fast memorization of factual associations followed by slower development of linear truth separation.
Layer normalization is necessary for the linear separability of true and false representations.
The value matrix develops a block structure that enables sharpening of predictions for true sequences.
Experiments with Pythia-6.9B show similar two-phase dynamics in a large pretrained model.
papers.limitation:
The toy model is far simpler than natural training data, so the mechanism might not fully capture real-world complexity.
In real LMs, additional mechanisms likely contribute to truth encoding.
future_direction: Systematic study of mechanisms for truth encoding in real LMs.
Generalization of truth encoding across different relations.
papers.abstract: Recent probing studies reveal that large language models exhibit linear subspaces that separate true from false statements, yet the mechanism behind their emergence is unclear. We introduce a transparent, one-layer transformer toy model that reproduces such truth subspaces end-to-end and exposes one concrete route by which they can arise. We study one simple setting in which truth encoding can emerge: a data distribution where factual statements co-occur with other factual statements (and vice-versa), encouraging the model to learn this distinction in order to lower the LM loss on future tokens. We corroborate this pattern with experiments in pretrained language models. Finally, in the toy setting we observe a two-phase learning dynamic: networks first memorize individual factual associations in a few steps, then -- over a longer horizon -- learn to linearly separate true from false, which in turn lowers language-modeling loss. Together, these results provide both a mechanistic demonstration and an empirical motivation for how and why linear truth representations can emerge in language models.

papers.title: What Do Llamas Really Think? Revealing Preference Biases in Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) exhibit sociodemographic biases, even when they decline to respond?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a new logistic Bradley-Terry probe for detecting implicit association bias in LLM representations, and uses it to reveal substantial sociodemographic biases in the embeddings of various LLMs, showing that instruction fine-tuning does not eliminate these latent biases.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a novel method for assessing implicit preference bias in LLM representations and concludes that instruction fine-tuning insufficiently removes latent bias, extending previous findings on shallow word embeddings to contextualized embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed logistic Bradley-Terry probe outperforms WEAT and max-margin classification by a relative 27-34% in error rate on preference prediction tasks.
Middle layers of the LLMs yield the best probes for preference detection.
LLMs exhibit implicit biases in nationality, politics, religion, and gender, favoring Western over Eastern countries, left-wing over right-wing ideologies, Christianity and Judaism over Islam, and female-prefixed careers over male-prefixed ones.
Instruction fine-tuning does not remove bias from the contextualized embeddings of LLMs.
CodeLLaMA models show less bias, likely due to additional pretraining on code.
future_direction: Thoroughly debias contextual word representations and reduce detectable bias.
Assess implicit bias in LLMs pretrained on different corpora and probe the effects of pretraining text choices on bias.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) exhibit sociodemographic biases, even when they decline to respond? To bypass their refusal to "speak," we study this research question by probing contextualized embeddings and exploring whether this bias is encoded in its latent representations. We propose a logistic Bradley-Terry probe which predicts word pair preferences of LLMs from the words' hidden vectors. We first validate our probe on three pair preference tasks and thirteen LLMs, where we outperform the word embedding association test (WEAT), a standard approach in testing for implicit association, by a relative 27% in error rate. We also find that word pair preferences are best represented in the middle layers. Next, we transfer probes trained on harmless tasks (e.g., pick the larger number) to controversial ones (compare ethnicities) to examine biases in nationality, politics, religion, and gender. We observe substantial bias for all target classes: for instance, the Mistral model implicitly prefers Europe to Africa, Christianity to Judaism, and left-wing to right-wing politics, despite declining to answer. This suggests that instruction fine-tuning does not necessarily debias contextualized embeddings. Our codebase is at https://github.com/castorini/biasprobe.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Bias Mitigation: An Interpretable Approach to Safer LLMs
papers.research_question: Can bias in large language models be detected and mitigated by probing internal activations and applying steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretability-based system that uses linear probes to detect bias in LLM activations and applies steering vectors to mitigate biased outputs in real-time.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that bias can be detected and mitigated through activation steering, offering a transparent method for improving LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on internal activations can detect bias with near-perfect accuracy in later layers of gpt2-large.
Bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers, as shown by increasing probe accuracy.
Steering vectors computed from activation differences can successfully alter biased completions toward more neutral alternatives during inference.
The method provides a direct and interpretable approach to bias mitigation without modifying model weights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted only on gpt2-large, limiting generalizability to other models.
The training dataset is synthetic, which may not fully represent real-world bias.
future_direction: Investigate whether findings generalize to other model architectures and sizes (e.g., Llama, Mistral).
Validate techniques on real-world datasets of hate speech or bias (e.g., HateXplain, CivilComments).
Explore the use of non-linear probes or more sophisticated steering techniques for more precise control.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more integrated into societal systems, the risk of them perpetuating and amplifying harmful biases becomes a critical safety concern. Traditional methods for mitigating bias often rely on data filtering or post-hoc output moderation, which treat the model as an opaque black box. In this work, we introduce a complete, end-to-end system that uses techniques from mechanistic interpretability to both identify and actively mitigate bias directly within a model's internal workings. Our method involves two primary stages. First, we train linear "probes" on the internal activations of a model to detect the latent representations of various biases (e.g., gender, race, age). Our experiments on \texttt{gpt2-large} demonstrate that these probes can identify biased content with near-perfect accuracy, revealing that bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers. Second, we leverage these findings to compute "steering vectors" by contrasting the model's activation patterns for biased and neutral statements. By adding these vectors during inference, we can actively steer the model's generative process away from producing harmful, stereotypical, or biased content in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of this activation steering technique, showing that it successfully alters biased completions toward more neutral alternatives. We present our work as a robust and reproducible system that offers a more direct and interpretable approach to building safer and more accountable LLMs.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, and how effective is this method?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method for steering language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, which effectively steers behavior, works on top of finetuning and system prompts, and minimally reduces capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behavior with minimal performance degradation, and offers insights into the linear representations of abstract concepts in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CAA can effectively steer Llama 2 Chat models on a variety of alignment-relevant behaviors (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal).
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks.
CAA can be combined with system prompting and finetuning to further control behavior.
CAA has minimal impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU.
The steering vectors correspond intuitively to the presence of the behavior in the generated tokens (as shown by cosine similarity).
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluation has limitations (sensitivity to prompt wording, biases).
Finetuning baseline was not fully optimized (hyperparameters, loss function).
Prompting baseline may not be fully optimized.
Vector normalization choices (norms vary across layers and behaviors).
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions (instead of all tokens after the prompt).
Steering outside the residual stream (e.g., after MLP).
Application to red-teaming (using CAA to trigger unwanted behaviors).
papers.abstract: Nina Rimsky, Nick Gabrieli, Julian Schulz, Meg Tong, Evan Hubinger, Alexander Turner. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Cyclic Ablation: Testing Concept Localization against Functional Regeneration in AI
