papers.core_contribution: Introduces mechanistic forecasting, a method that aggregates internal model activations (specifically party-aligned MLP value vectors) to predict human preferences, demonstrating that latent representations often contain more accurate information than surface-level output probabilities for election forecasting.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode latent information about human preferences not fully expressed in output probabilities, and aggregating this information via mechanistic forecasting can improve preference predictions in many settings, establishing a new approach for using LLMs in social science.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic forecasting improves prediction accuracy over probability-based estimation across multiple models and national election contexts.
Linear probes trained on residual stream representations reliably capture political party associations with high F1 scores.
Estimation error varies by political party, with latent information providing the greatest gains for parties harder to predict from probabilities.
Demographic persona attributes (e.g., age, education) benefit more consistently from latent representations than opinion-based attributes, which show greater cross-national variation.
Attribute-level entropy of output probability distributions can serve as a gating criterion for when to prefer mechanistic forecasting over probability-based prediction.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is restricted to white-box models, excluding black-box models common in practice.
Method requires training probes for each party and country, adding computational overhead.
Results are based on a limited set of elections and may not generalize to other contexts.
future_direction: Extend approach to black-box models via gradient-based approximations.
Apply mechanistic forecasting to other preference domains beyond elections.
Investigate the interaction between latent representations and model alignment.
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to predict human preferences in both scientific and business endeavors, yet current approaches rely exclusively on analyzing model outputs without considering the underlying mechanisms. Using election forecasting as a test case, we introduce mechanistic forecasting, a method that demonstrates that probing internal model representations offers a fundamentally different - and sometimes more effective - approach to preference prediction. Examining over 24 million configurations across 7 models, 6 national elections, multiple persona attributes, and prompt variations, we systematically analyze how demographic and ideological information activates latent party-encoding components within the respective models. We find that leveraging this internal knowledge via mechanistic forecasting (opposed to solely relying on surface-level predictions) can improve prediction accuracy. The effects vary across demographic versus opinion-based attributes, political parties, national contexts, and models. Our findings demonstrate that the latent representational structure of LLMs contains systematic, exploitable information about human preferences, establishing a new path for using language models in social science prediction tasks.

papers.title: Codebook Features: Sparse and Discrete Interpretability for Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can we train neural networks to have hidden states that are sparse, discrete, and more interpretable by quantizing their continuous features into codebook features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces codebook features, a method to make neural network hidden states sparse and discrete via vector quantization bottlenecks, enabling improved interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: Codebook features are a promising unit of analysis and control for neural networks, providing a sparse, discrete interface for understanding and steering model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can operate with extreme sparse, discrete bottlenecks at each layer with only modest performance degradation.
In a finite state machine task, codebooks overcome superposition by assigning distinct states to discrete codes, and activating a state's code causes the network to behave as if in that state.
In language models, codebooks learn codes representing diverse, disentangled concepts (e.g., topics, emotions, syntax).
Activating topic-related codes during inference can steer language model generations towards those topics.
Codes are better classifiers of simple textual features than individual neurons in the network.
papers.limitation:
Codebook models exhibit modest degradation in performance compared to the original models.
In larger models, many codes do not have a comprehensible interpretation.
future_direction: Understanding circuits and weights by leveraging the sparse, discrete nature of codebooks.
Understanding adversarial examples by identifying which codes shift to cause misclassifications.
Improving interpretability in larger models by using larger codebooks or analyzing code co-occurrence.
Understanding shared representations across domains and modalities (e.g., text and image).
papers.abstract: Understanding neural networks is challenging in part because of the dense, continuous nature of their hidden states. We explore whether we can train neural networks to have hidden states that are sparse, discrete, and more interpretable by quantizing their continuous features into what we call codebook features. Codebook features are produced by finetuning neural networks with vector quantization bottlenecks at each layer, producing a network whose hidden features are the sum of a small number of discrete vector codes chosen from a larger codebook. Surprisingly, we find that neural networks can operate under this extreme bottleneck with only modest degradation in performance. This sparse, discrete bottleneck also provides an intuitive way of controlling neural network behavior: first, find codes that activate when the desired behavior is present, then activate those same codes during generation to elicit that behavior. We validate our approach by training codebook Transformers on several different datasets. First, we explore a finite state machine dataset with far more hidden states than neurons. In this setting, our approach overcomes the superposition problem by assigning states to distinct codes, and we find that we can make the neural network behave as if it is in a different state by activating the code for that state. Second, we train Transformer language models with up to 410M parameters on two natural language datasets. We identify codes in these models representing diverse, disentangled concepts (ranging from negative emotions to months of the year) and find that we can guide the model to generate different topics by activating the appropriate codes during inference. Overall, codebook features appear to be a promising unit of analysis and control for neural networks and interpretability. Our codebase and models are open-sourced at https://github.com/taufeeque9/codebook-features.

papers.title: Local Convolutions Cause an Implicit Bias towards High Frequency Adversarial Examples
papers.research_question: Why do adversarial perturbations typically contain high-frequency features? The paper hypothesizes that convolutional operations with localized kernels are implicitly biased to learn high frequency features, which is a root cause of high frequency adversarial examples.
papers.core_contribution: Local convolutions cause an implicit bias towards high frequency features, which leads to high frequency adversarial examples. This is demonstrated through experiments and theoretical analysis, showing that the bias is due to the Fourier Uncertainty Principle and translation invariance.
papers.conclusion: Local convolutions are a root cause of high frequency adversarial examples, and understanding architectural implicit bias is essential for adversarial robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Full-width convolutional models induce a sparsity-promoting regularizer in the frequency domain, leading to sparser frequency spectra in learned features and adversarial perturbations.
Bounded-width convolutional models show a bias towards high frequency features, which increases with smaller kernel sizes due to the Fourier Uncertainty Principle.
Translation invariance (weight sharing) in convolutions is necessary for the high frequency bias; locally connected models without weight sharing do not exhibit the same bias.
Vision Transformers and other non-convolutional architectures (e.g., MLPMixer) have adversarial perturbations with more energy in lower frequencies compared to convolutional models.
The implicit bias of convolutional architectures affects feature learning, as shown by steganography experiments where convolutional models better utilize high-frequency shortcut features.
papers.limitation: Full-width convolutional layers are not often used in common state-of-the-art architectures, so the analysis of full-width convolutions may not directly apply to practical models.
future_direction: Probe the ability of models to generalize along any basis, not just Fourier.
Establish the relationship between implicit bias due to model parametrization and robustness to different input perturbations.
Understand and control the implicit bias of architectures for adversarial robustness.
papers.abstract: Adversarial Attacks are still a significant challenge for neural networks. Recent work has shown that adversarial perturbations typically contain high-frequency features, but the root cause of this phenomenon remains unknown. Inspired by theoretical work on linear full-width convolutional models, we hypothesize that the local (i.e. bounded-width) convolutional operations commonly used in current neural networks are implicitly biased to learn high frequency features, and that this is one of the root causes of high frequency adversarial examples. To test this hypothesis, we analyzed the impact of different choices of linear and nonlinear architectures on the implicit bias of the learned features and the adversarial perturbations, in both spatial and frequency domains. We find that the high-frequency adversarial perturbations are critically dependent on the convolution operation because the spatially-limited nature of local convolutions induces an implicit bias towards high frequency features. The explanation for the latter involves the Fourier Uncertainty Principle: a spatially-limited (local in the space domain) filter cannot also be frequency-limited (local in the frequency domain). Furthermore, using larger convolution kernel sizes or avoiding convolutions (e.g. by using Vision Transformers architecture) significantly reduces this high frequency bias, but not the overall susceptibility to attacks. Looking forward, our work strongly suggests that understanding and controlling the implicit bias of architectures will be essential for achieving adversarial robustness.

papers.title: Interpreting CLIP's Image Representation via Text-Based Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can we interpret CLIP's image representation by decomposing it into contributions from individual model components (attention heads and image patches) using text-based explanations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to interpret CLIP's image representation via text-based decomposition into attention heads and image patches, enabling improved zero-shot segmentation and reduction of spurious correlations.
papers.conclusion: Scalable understanding of transformer models is attainable and can be used to repair and improve models.
papers.key_findings:
The direct effect on the output is concentrated in the last 4 MSA layers.
TEXT SPAN reveals property-specific roles for many attention heads (e.g., location, shape, color).
Decomposition into image tokens yields a zero-shot segmenter that outperforms existing methods.
Removing heads associated with spurious cues improves worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds from 48% to 73%.
Joint decomposition visualizes which image regions contribute to specific text directions, validating the text labels.
papers.limitation:
Only direct effects are analyzed, not indirect effects.
Not all attention heads have clear roles.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other CLIP architectures (e.g., ResNet).
Use insights to design better CLIP image encoders and feature extractors for downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: We investigate the CLIP image encoder by analyzing how individual model components affect the final representation. We decompose the image representation as a sum across individual image patches, model layers, and attention heads, and use CLIP's text representation to interpret the summands. Interpreting the attention heads, we characterize each head's role by automatically finding text representations that span its output space, which reveals property-specific roles for many heads (e.g. location or shape). Next, interpreting the image patches, we uncover an emergent spatial localization within CLIP. Finally, we use this understanding to remove spurious features from CLIP and to create a strong zero-shot image segmenter. Our results indicate that a scalable understanding of transformer models is attainable and can be used to repair and improve models.

papers.title: Interpreting Arithmetic Mechanism in Large Language Models through Comparative Neuron Analysis
papers.research_question: How is arithmetic ability implemented in large language models, specifically the role of attention heads and FFN neurons, and what is the internal logic chain from input to prediction? Additionally, how does the LoRA fine-tuning method work?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method to interpret arithmetic mechanisms in LLMs, identifying an internal logic chain of four stages, and applies it to understand LoRA and for model pruning and bias reduction.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies important attention heads and FFN neurons for arithmetic, proposes the CNA method to construct the internal logic chain, finds LoRA amplifies important FFN neurons, and applies CNA to model pruning and editing.
papers.key_findings:
Arithmetic ability is localized in a few attention heads (arithmetic heads), each specializing in distinct operations.
The internal logic chain from input to prediction consists of four stages: feature enhancing, feature transferring, feature predicting, and prediction enhancing.
LoRA enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of important FFN neurons related to the final prediction.
Model pruning retaining only 5% of deep FFN neurons identified by CNA maintains performance on arithmetic tasks.
Model editing by zeroing 18 FFN neurons identified by CNA reduces gender bias by 35.7%.
papers.limitation:
The case studies rely on projecting vectors in vocabulary space, which is empirically interpretable but lacks complete theoretical foundation.
There is a lack of standardization across various studies regarding attribution methods (e.g., different intervention methods).
A potential risk is that attackers can identify and edit important neurons to change model behavior maliciously.
future_direction: Further investigation of the multiplication heads which do not significantly impact accuracy.
Explorations on different datasets for gender bias reduction.
Distinguishing whether a model has been edited to prevent malicious use.

papers.title: GPT and Prejudice: A Sparse Approach to Understanding Learned Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we trace how different social patterns and biases from pretraining data are encoded in the internal representations of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pipeline that couples LLMs with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to audit how cultural assumptions and biases from training data are embedded in model representations, demonstrated via a case study on 19th-century novels.
papers.conclusion: The LLM+SAEs pipeline provides a systematic method for exploring cultural and social patterns embedded in corpora, bridging interpretability research and corpus analysis, and is adaptable for applications from literary analysis to fairness auditing.
papers.key_findings:
The model encodes social and moral themes from the corpus, with gender and kinship forming a stable conceptual backbone across layers.
Early layers contain few but relatively pure concept detectors, mid-layers balance clarity and capacity, and deeper layers host more neurons that are increasingly entangled across multiple concepts.
The male category produces the purest, most selective detectors, while female functions as a relational hub, connecting to nearly every other major concept.
The pipeline can be adapted to different domains (e.g., HR, healthcare) by customizing the probing concepts, offering a scalable framework for bias auditing and corpus analysis.
papers.limitation: The results are shaped by the design of the probing dataset and the chosen concepts; other categories might yield different insights.
future_direction: Applying the pipeline to larger, more diverse corpora.
Extending the probing concepts to test different conceptual frames.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on massive, unstructured corpora, making it unclear which social patterns and biases they absorb and later reproduce. Existing evaluations typically examine outputs or activations, but rarely connect them back to the pre-training data. We introduce a pipeline that couples LLMs with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to trace how different themes are encoded during training. As a controlled case study, we trained a GPT-style model on 37 nineteenth-century novels by ten female authors, a corpus centered on themes such as gender, marriage, class, and morality. By applying SAEs across layers and probing with eleven social and moral categories, we mapped sparse features to human-interpretable concepts. The analysis revealed stable thematic backbones (most prominently around gender and kinship) and showed how associations expand and entangle with depth. More broadly, we argue that the LLM+SAEs pipeline offers a scalable framework for auditing how cultural assumptions from the data are embedded in model representations.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Mechanistic Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we control large language models by understanding their inner working mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of language models can be leveraged to control their behavior in various applications, such as reducing hallucination, improving instruction stability, and enhancing planning in dialogues.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation shows that mechanistic control is a promising approach for aligning language models, and future work should expand the scope of interpretability and control to more complex behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns an emergent world representation of the Othello board, and this representation can be intervened on to edit the model's perceived world state.
Inference-time intervention (ITI) can elicit more truthful answers from language models by shifting activations along truthful directions found in attention heads.
Instruction drift in long conversations is caused by attention decay, and split-softmax can mitigate this drift by forcing the model to pay more attention to the system prompt.
Dialogue action tokens (DAT) enable better planning in multi-turn dialogues by using a planner to predict action vectors that steer the language model towards long-horizon goals.
papers.abstract: This dissertation talks about mechanistic control of large language models (LLM). The intuition is that, in order to rigorously control large language models, it is beneficial to first understand their inner working mechanisms. Even though a fully mechanistic understanding of language models is far from complete at the time this dissertation is written, I will demonstrate several cases where such understanding provides a useful surface for control. I argue that connecting interpretability to real-life applications--e.g., alignment and safety--offers advantages to the development of both fields. I first position this methodological approach within a broader scientific context, discussing and systematizing the role of interpretability in artificial intelligence research. I then present four intensive case studies, each leveraging certain interpretability insights to control the behavior of language models. The interpretability insights I explored span emergent world representations, representation of internal knowledge, phenomenon of attention decay, and representation of users. The demonstrated effects of control include targeted editing of the world model, reduced hallucination, improved stability of system prompts in long conversations, and better planning in multi-turn dialogue.

papers.title: Neural Transparency: Mechanistic Interpretability Interfaces for Anticipating Model Behaviors for Personalized AI
papers.research_question: Can neural transparency tools, which translate mechanistic interpretability insights into user-facing interfaces, help users anticipate and design safer AI chatbot behaviors from system prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neural transparency interface that translates mechanistic interpretability insights (persona vectors derived from neural activations) into an actionable tool for non-technical users to predict chatbot personality traits from system prompts before deployment.
papers.conclusion: Neural transparency visualizations can increase user trust and enhance the subjective experience of the AI design process, offering a path to operationalize mechanistic interpretability for end-users to support safer, more aligned human-AI interactions.
papers.key_findings:
Users systematically miscalibrated their predictions of AI behavior, misjudging trait activations for 11 of 15 analyzable traits, highlighting the need for transparency tools.
The neural transparency interface significantly increased user trust in the AI model and was enthusiastically received, though it did not change design iteration patterns.
Persona vectors (linear directions in activation space) for traits like empathy, sociality, and toxicity showed strong linear relationships with synthetic prompt levels, validating the approach for most traits.
papers.limitation:
Relied on GPT-4.1-mini to evaluate trait expression in Llama responses, which may not fully capture human judgments of trait expression.
The persona vector generation method uses simple difference-in-means, prioritizing efficiency over the potential accuracy/robustness of more complex techniques like linear probes.
The 10-minute interaction period may not capture longer-term dynamics of chatbot relationships where problematic interactions typically emerge.
Participants' inaccurate trait predictions may be partly due to transforming coarse ordinal prediction data to normalized values, potentially making predictions more extreme.
future_direction: Longitudinal deployment studies to track users across multiple chatbot creation sessions.
Adversarial task conditions where transparency tools become necessary to avoid dangerous traits.
Active steering interfaces allowing users to directly manipulate persona vector activations.
Development of a standardized trait disclosure framework (like a 'nutritional label') for chatbots.
Studies with vulnerable populations (e.g., adolescents) most at risk from problematic chatbot relationships.
papers.abstract: Millions of users now design personalized LLM-based chatbots that shape their daily interactions, yet they can only roughly anticipate how their design choices will manifest as behaviors in deployment. This opacity is consequential: seemingly innocuous prompts can trigger excessive sycophancy, toxicity, or other undesirable traits, degrading utility and raising safety concerns. To address this issue, we introduce an interface that enables neural transparency by exposing language model internals during chatbot design. Our approach extracts behavioral trait vectors (empathy, toxicity, sycophancy, etc.) by computing differences in neural activations between contrastive system prompts that elicit opposing behaviors. We predict chatbot behaviors by projecting the system prompt's final token activations onto these trait vectors, normalizing for cross-trait comparability, and visualizing results via an interactive sunburst diagram. To evaluate this approach, we conducted an online user study using Prolific to compare our neural transparency interface against a baseline chatbot interface without any form of transparency. Our analyses suggest that users systematically miscalibrated AI behavior: participants misjudged trait activations for eleven of fifteen analyzable traits, motivating the need for transparency tools in everyday human-AI interaction. While our interface did not change design iteration patterns, it significantly increased user trust and was enthusiastically received. Qualitative analysis revealed nuanced user experiences with the visualization, suggesting interface and interaction improvements for future work. This work offers a path for how mechanistic interpretability can be operationalized for non-technical users, establishing a foundation for safer, more aligned human-AI interactions.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Localizing Lying in Llama: Understanding Instructed Dishonesty on True-False Questions Through Prompting, Probing, and Patching
papers.research_question: How can instructed dishonesty (lying) in a large language model be localized and understood using mechanistic interpretability methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper localizes layers and attention heads responsible for instructed dishonesty in LLaMA-2-70b-chat, showing that causal interventions on just 46 heads can flip the model's behavior from lying to answering honestly.
papers.conclusion: The work contributes to understanding dishonesty in LLMs by localizing the behavior to specific layers and heads, enabling causal interventions that flip the model from lying to honesty, with the goal of informing methods to prevent such behavior.
papers.key_findings:
LLaMA-2-70b-chat can be instructed to lie on true/false questions, but this behavior is sensitive and requires careful prompt engineering, including the use of assistant response prefixes.
Linear probing and activation patching identify layers 19-23 as crucial for dishonest behavior, with representations between honest and liar prompts becoming anti-parallel after these layers.
Activation patching from an honest model into a lying model on layers 19-23 can significantly increase the liar's accuracy from 2% to 63%.
A subset of 46 attention heads within layers 19-23 (0.9% of all heads) is causally important for lying; patching these heads from honest to liar models flips the liar's behavior to be honest, and vice versa.
The intervention on the 46 heads generalizes robustly across different prompts and dataset splits (Cities, Inventions, Chemical Elements, Animals, Companies, Scientific Facts).
papers.limitation: The analysis is in a toy scenario where lying involves outputting a one-token incorrect response; realistic lying scenarios could involve arbitrarily misaligned optimization targets.
future_direction: Analyze more complex misalignments (e.g., swaying political beliefs, selling products) using similar methods to find where biases/misalignments exist.
Further mechanistic interpretability work to understand how the model elicits a truth-value representation and uses it with the system prompt to decide whether to respond truthfully.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate significant knowledge through their outputs, though it is often unclear whether false outputs are due to a lack of knowledge or dishonesty. In this paper, we investigate instructed dishonesty, wherein we explicitly prompt LLaMA-2-70b-chat to lie. We perform prompt engineering to find which prompts best induce lying behavior, and then use mechanistic interpretability approaches to localize where in the network this behavior occurs. Using linear probing and activation patching, we localize five layers that appear especially important for lying. We then find just 46 attention heads within these layers that enable us to causally intervene such that the lying model instead answers honestly. We show that these interventions work robustly across many prompts and dataset splits. Overall, our work contributes a greater understanding of dishonesty in LLMs so that we may hope to prevent it.

papers.title: Understanding CNN fragility when learning with imbalanced data
papers.research_question: Why do CNNs struggle to generalize to minority classes when trained on imbalanced data, and how can we understand this by analyzing latent features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that CNNs learn less diverse latent features for minority classes, relying on fewer but higher magnitude features, which explains their fragility and poor generalization on imbalanced data.
papers.conclusion: The analysis of latent features (FE and CE) provides insights into why CNNs struggle with minority classes, highlighting the importance of feature diversity and magnitude matching for generalization.
papers.key_findings:
CNN minority class latent features are less diverse than majority classes.
CNN minority class predictions rely on fewer, higher magnitude relevant features.
This higher response and lower diversity leads to poor generalization.
A CNN generalizes well only if the range of top-K latent feature magnitudes matches between training and test sets.
Cost-sensitive algorithms (LDAM, Focal loss) do not fundamentally change the diversity of learned features.
papers.limitation: The study uses only three image datasets and random sampling may introduce variability.
future_direction: Investigating the impact of data augmentation techniques (like SMOTE) on latent feature diversity.
Visualizing latent features to discover methods for better disentanglement of class representations.
Assessing more datasets with multiple cross-validation runs to solidify results.
papers.abstract: Abstract Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved impressive results on imbalanced image data, but they still have difficulty generalizing to minority classes and their decisions are difficult to interpret. These problems are related because the method by which CNNs generalize to minority classes, which requires improvement, is wrapped in a black-box. To demystify CNN decisions on imbalanced data, we focus on their latent features. Although CNNs embed the pattern knowledge learned from a training set in model parameters, the effect of this knowledge is contained in feature and classification embeddings ( FE and CE ). These embeddings can be extracted from a trained model and their global, class properties (e.g., frequency, magnitude and identity) can be analyzed. We find that important information regarding the ability of a neural network to generalize to minority classes resides in the class top-K CE and FE . We show that a CNN learns a limited number of class top-K CE per category, and that their magnitudes vary based on whether the same class is balanced or imbalanced. We hypothesize that latent class diversity is as important as the number of class examples, which has important implications for re-sampling and cost-sensitive methods. These methods generally focus on rebalancing model weights, class numbers and margins; instead of diversifying class latent features. We also demonstrate that a CNN has difficulty generalizing to test data if the magnitude of its top-K latent features do not match the training set. We use three popular image datasets and two cost-sensitive algorithms commonly employed in imbalanced learning for our experiments.

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that circuit discovery and activation steering are dual operations on the same geometric structure encoded in activation space, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and effective steering, and revealing transformer circuits as geometric objects.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit membership can be determined from geometric alignment with answer token directions, recovering circuit structure comparable to gradient-based methods without backpropagation.
The same directions enable controlled steering, validating that they manipulate genuine computational pathways.
Feature circuits can be discovered by extracting directions from instruction-modified prompts, without task-specific datasets.
The method achieves comparable circuit discovery performance to gradient-based methods (EAP, EAP-IG) on IOI, SVA, and MCQA tasks across four model families.
Steering using these directions achieves 69.8% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy (89.6%).
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot steering remains fragile; even grammatically correct outputs can exhibit semantic degradation.
Steering can disrupt factual recall, particularly for negative-valence emotions and distant language pairs, suggesting some features remain entangled with semantic content.
future_direction: Address position-level effects beyond the final token.
Address LayerNorm nonlinearities in edge attribution.
Develop methods to preserve factual grounding during steering.
Develop more robust persona-based circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery and activation steering in transformers have developed as separate research threads, yet both operate on the same representational space. Are they two views of the same underlying structure? We show they follow a single geometric principle: answer tokens, processed in isolation, encode the directions that would produce them. This Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis enables circuit discovery without gradients or causal intervention -- recovering comparable structure to gradient-based methods through geometric alignment alone. We validate this on standard benchmarks (IOI, SVA, MCQA) across four model families, achieving circuit discovery performance comparable to gradient-based methods. The same directions that identify circuit components also enable controlled steering -- achieving 69.8\% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1\% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy. Beyond method development, this read-write duality reveals that transformer circuits are fundamentally geometric structures: interpretability and controllability are two facets of the same object.

papers.title: Aligned but Blind: Alignment Increases Implicit Bias by Reducing Awareness of Race
papers.research_question: How does alignment in language models lead to increased implicit bias by reducing awareness of race?
papers.core_contribution: Alignment in language models increases implicit bias by reducing awareness of race in ambiguous contexts, and a mitigation strategy that incentivizes race representation in early layers effectively reduces this bias.
papers.conclusion: Value-aligned LMs exhibit implicit bias in ambiguous contexts due to race blindness, and interventions that increase race awareness can mitigate this bias, highlighting limitations in current alignment methods.
papers.key_findings:
Alignment reduces explicit bias to near zero but significantly increases implicit bias in word association tasks.
Aligned models fail to represent racial concepts in ambiguous contexts, treating polysemous words like 'black' and 'white' as color rather than race.
Activation patching shows that aligned models are less likely to interpret race in ambiguous prompts, indicating race blindness.
Interventions that inject race-laden activations or fine-tune models to associate ambiguous words with race reduce implicit bias.
Early layer interventions are more effective than later layers for bias mitigation.
papers.limitation:
Focused solely on racial biases using the ambiguity of black and white in Llama 3 models.
Mechanistic interpretations are influenced by model architecture, data, and interpretability methods, and are limited by human-defined concepts.
Amplifying race associations may have side effects beyond bias metrics examined.
Qualitative comparisons to human race blindness may not fully capture psychological motivations.
future_direction: Extend the approach to other types of social bias, such as gender bias.
Investigate the origins of the associations between color and concepts in pretraining.
Study more tokens with ambiguity in broader contexts across different model families.
papers.abstract: Although value-aligned language models (LMs) appear unbiased in explicit bias evaluations, they often exhibit stereotypes in implicit word association tasks, raising concerns about their fair usage. We investigate the mechanisms behind this discrepancy and find that alignment surprisingly amplifies implicit bias in model outputs. Specifically, we show that aligned LMs, unlike their unaligned counterparts, overlook racial concepts in early internal representations when the context is ambiguous. Not representing race likely fails to activate safety guardrails, leading to unintended biases. Inspired by this insight, we propose a new bias mitigation strategy that works by incentivizing the representation of racial concepts in the early model layers. In contrast to conventional mitigation methods of machine unlearning, our interventions find that steering the model to be more aware of racial concepts effectively mitigates implicit bias. Similar to race blindness in humans, ignoring racial nuances can inadvertently perpetuate subtle biases in LMs.

papers.title: The Devil is in the Neurons: Interpreting and Mitigating Social Biases in Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: How to precisely identify the social bias neurons in PLMs? How to effectively mitigate social biases in PLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of social bias neurons, proposes Integrated Gap Gradients (IG2) to identify them, and derives Bias Neuron Suppression (BNS) to mitigate social biases in pre-trained language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes IG2 for interpreting social bias neurons and BNS for mitigating social biases, with experimental verification and analysis providing insights for future fairness research.
papers.key_findings:
IG2 accurately pinpoints social bias neurons in PLMs, as verified by suppression and amplification experiments.
Suppressing social bias neurons reduces bias, while amplifying them increases bias.
BNS effectively mitigates social biases while preserving language modeling ability, outperforming baseline methods.
Social bias neurons are concentrated in the deepest layers of BERT and RoBERTa; after debiasing (FairBERTa), they shift to shallower layers.
Different demographic dimensions have varying numbers of social bias neurons, with 'Ethnicity' having the most and 'Gender' the fewest.
papers.limitation: The BNS method directly sets the activation values of selected social bias neurons to zero, which, while effective, might be improved by a more refined suppression method.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained Language models (PLMs) have been acknowledged to contain harmful information, such as social biases, which may cause negative social impacts or even bring catastrophic results in application. Previous works on this problem mainly focused on using black-box methods such as probing to detect and quantify social biases in PLMs by observing model outputs. As a result, previous debiasing methods mainly finetune or even pre-train language models on newly constructed anti-stereotypical datasets, which are high-cost. In this work, we try to unveil the mystery of social bias inside language models by introducing the concept of {\sc Social Bias Neurons}. Specifically, we propose {\sc Integrated Gap Gradients (IG$^2$)} to accurately pinpoint units (i.e., neurons) in a language model that can be attributed to undesirable behavior, such as social bias. By formalizing undesirable behavior as a distributional property of language, we employ sentiment-bearing prompts to elicit classes of sensitive words (demographics) correlated with such sentiments. Our IG$^2$ thus attributes the uneven distribution for different demographics to specific Social Bias Neurons, which track the trail of unwanted behavior inside PLM units to achieve interoperability. Moreover, derived from our interpretable technique, {\sc Bias Neuron Suppression (BNS)} is further proposed to mitigate social biases. By studying BERT, RoBERTa, and their attributable differences from debiased FairBERTa, IG$^2$ allows us to locate and suppress identified neurons, and further mitigate undesired behaviors. As measured by prior metrics from StereoSet, our model achieves a higher degree of fairness while maintaining language modeling ability with low cost.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: The Mechanistic Emergence of Symbol Grounding in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does symbol grounding emerge in language models, specifically what are the loci and mechanisms driving this emergence?
papers.core_contribution: Symbol grounding emerges in middle-layer computations via aggregate attention heads that retrieve environmental grounds to predict linguistic forms, generalizing across Transformers and state-space models but not LSTMs.
papers.conclusion: Symbol grounding can mechanistically emerge in autoregressive language models, with practical implications for predicting and potentially controlling the reliability of generation.
papers.key_findings:
Grounding concentrates in middle-layer computations.
Grounding is implemented through an aggregate mechanism where attention heads aggregate environmental ground to support prediction of linguistic forms.
This phenomenon replicates in multimodal dialogue and across architectures (Transformers and state-space models) but not in unidirectional LSTMs.
Grounding cannot be fully explained by co-occurrence statistics.
Causal interventions show that aggregate heads are critical for grounding.
papers.limitation: Full-scale VLMs present additional complications such as large numbers of visual tokens and redundant artifact tokens, making systematic identification and intervention at scale a nontrivial challenge.
future_direction: Investigate how grounding mechanisms interact with other emergent phenomena, such as in-context learning and reasoning.
Scale the analysis to larger models and more naturalistic settings.
papers.abstract: Symbol grounding (Harnad, 1990) describes how symbols such as words acquire their meanings by connecting to real-world sensorimotor experiences. Recent work has shown preliminary evidence that grounding may emerge in (vision-)language models trained at scale without using explicit grounding objectives. Yet, the specific loci of this emergence and the mechanisms that drive it remain largely unexplored. To address this problem, we introduce a controlled evaluation framework that systematically traces how symbol grounding arises within the internal computations through mechanistic and causal analysis. Our findings show that grounding concentrates in middle-layer computations and is implemented through the aggregate mechanism, where attention heads aggregate the environmental ground to support the prediction of linguistic forms. This phenomenon replicates in multimodal dialogue and across architectures (Transformers and state-space models), but not in unidirectional LSTMs. Our results provide behavioral and mechanistic evidence that symbol grounding can emerge in language models, with practical implications for predicting and potentially controlling the reliability of generation.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Lost in Translation: The Algorithmic Gap Between LMs and the Brain
papers.research_question: What is the algorithmic gap between language models and the human brain, and how can we bridge it?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that despite computational-level equivalence in some tasks, language models diverge from human cognition at the algorithmic level, and proposes neuroscience-inspired architectural and training changes to bridge this gap.
papers.conclusion: The intelligence emerging from current LMs is fundamentally different from human cognition, and incorporating brain-inspired constraints may lead to AI with human-like flexibility and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Language models and the brain show representational similarities but likely use different algorithms.
Current LMs lack brain-like features such as sparsity, modularity, internal states, and interactive learning.
Incorporating brain-inspired features could lead to more human-like AI and better models of cognition.
future_direction: Incorporate sparse connectivity and modularity (e.g., MoE, RIMs) in LMs.
Add internal states and recurrence to transformers.
Develop continual and curriculum learning methods for LMs.
Ground LMs in embodied and social interactions.
Integrate oscillatory dynamics and scaling laws with efficiency constraints.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) have achieved impressive performance on various linguistic tasks, but their relationship to human language processing in the brain remains unclear. This paper examines the gaps and overlaps between LMs and the brain at different levels of analysis, emphasizing the importance of looking beyond input-output behavior to examine and compare the internal processes of these systems. We discuss how insights from neuroscience, such as sparsity, modularity, internal states, and interactive learning, can inform the development of more biologically plausible language models. Furthermore, we explore the role of scaling laws in bridging the gap between LMs and human cognition, highlighting the need for efficiency constraints analogous to those in biological systems. By developing LMs that more closely mimic brain function, we aim to advance both artificial intelligence and our understanding of human cognition.

papers.title: Implicit Representations of Meaning in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the effectiveness of neural language models derive entirely from accurate modeling of surface word co-occurrence statistics, or do these models represent and reason about the world they describe?
papers.core_contribution: Our results indicate that prediction in pre-trained neural language models is supported, at least in part, by dynamic representations of meaning and implicit simulation of entity state, and that this behavior can be learned with only text as training data.
papers.conclusion: Our results indicate that prediction in pre-trained neural language models is supported, at least in part, by dynamic representations of meaning and implicit simulation of entity state, and that this behavior can be learned with only text as training data.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic state information can be linearly decoded from NLM encodings of entity mentions.
This ability is primarily attributable to open-domain pre-training rather than in-domain fine-tuning.
Representations of entities are local to entity mentions, with the last mention encoding the most information.
Changes to entity representations (via intervention) cause predictable changes in language model predictions, indicating a causal role.
The implicit semantic models are approximate and error-prone, but exhibit functional similarities to formal dynamic semantics.
papers.limitation: The implicit semantic models are approximate and error-prone.
future_direction: More detailed exploration of quantification in NLMs.
Better methods for evaluating and improving factuality and coherence in NLMs.
papers.abstract: Belinda Z. Li, Maxwell Nye, Jacob Andreas. Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2021.

papers.title: The Vector Grounding Problem
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded in the world, i.e., have intrinsic meaning, despite being trained only on text data without direct interaction with the world?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that large language models can achieve referential grounding (intrinsic meaning) through selection processes in training that endow internal states with representational functions, even without multimodality or embodiment.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can, in principle and in some cases in practice, have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded, thus solving the Vector Grounding Problem and possessing intrinsic meaning independently of human interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Distinguishes referential grounding from other forms (sensorimotor, relational, communicative, epistemic) and argues referential grounding is the only kind essential to solving the Vector Grounding Problem.
Proposes that referential grounding requires two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories: causal-informational relations to the world and a history of selection that endows internal states with the function of carrying this information.
Argues that post-training (e.g., preference tuning for factual accuracy) can establish selection processes that confer world-involving representational functions to LLM internal states.
Suggests that pre-training might, under specific conditions, also lead to world-involving representational functions through implicit extra-linguistic success conditions in the training data.
Contends that in-context learning could, in principle, allow LLMs to acquire world-involving representational functions during inference without parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce seemingly meaningful outputs, yet they are trained on text alone without direct interaction with the world. This leads to a modern variant of the classical symbol grounding problem in AI: can LLMs' internal states and outputs be about extra-linguistic reality, independently of the meaning human interpreters project onto them? We argue that they can. We first distinguish referential grounding -- the connection between a representation and its worldly referent -- from other forms of grounding and argue it is the only kind essential to solving the problem. We contend that referential grounding is achieved when a system's internal states satisfy two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories of representation: (1) they stand in appropriate causal-informational relations to the world, and (2) they have a history of selection that has endowed them with the function of carrying this information. We argue that LLMs can meet both conditions, even without multimodality or embodiment.

papers.title: Neurobiological Causal Models of Language Processing
papers.research_question: How can we develop neurobiologically grounded causal models to explain the neural mechanisms of language processing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a neurobiological causal modeling framework to bridge the gap between language behavior and neural mechanisms, aiming for an integrated computational neurobiology of language.
papers.conclusion: Neurobiological causal modeling provides a unified framework for understanding language processing from first principles of neurobiology and should be actively pursued to integrate language across levels of explanation.
papers.key_findings:
Current cognitive and computational models of language lack explicit neurobiological foundations and need constraints from first principles of neurobiology.
Language processing can be formalized as an adaptive dynamical system built from neurobiological components, with processing and learning dynamics coupled through differential equations.
Hierarchical linguistic structure can be dynamically interpreted in terms of neural processing through function composition and memory, without requiring explicit tree representations.
The core computational machinery for language involves a mental lexicon for word storage and a unification network for combinatorial processing, both implemented in neurobiological infrastructure.
Neurobiological causal modeling should be pursued as a complementary approach to traditional methods to achieve an integrated understanding across levels of description.
future_direction: What are the elementary units of language in neurobiological terms?
What is the neurobiological correlate of processing memory for unification?
How is a language-specific mental lexicon acquired given weak neurophysiological learning mechanisms?
papers.abstract: The language faculty is physically realized in the neurobiological infrastructure of the human brain. Despite significant efforts, an integrated understanding of this system remains a formidable challenge. What is missing from most theoretical accounts is a specification of the neural mechanisms that implement language function. Computational models that have been put forward generally lack an explicit neurobiological foundation. We propose a neurobiologically informed causal modeling approach which offers a framework for how to bridge this gap. A neurobiological causal model is a mechanistic description of language processing that is grounded in, and constrained by, the characteristics of the neurobiological substrate. It intends to model the generators of language behavior at the level of implementational causality. We describe key features and neurobiological component parts from which causal models can be built and provide guidelines on how to implement them in model simulations. Then we outline how this approach can shed new light on the core computational machinery for language, the long-term storage of words in the mental lexicon and combinatorial processing in sentence comprehension. In contrast to cognitive theories of behavior, causal models are formulated in the "machine language" of neurobiology which is universal to human cognition. We argue that neurobiological causal modeling should be pursued in addition to existing approaches. Eventually, this approach will allow us to develop an explicit computational neurobiology of language.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language when processing non-English prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that multilingual language models like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate representations favoring English before shifting to the target language.
papers.conclusion: The evidence suggests that the abstract 'concept space' in multilingual transformers lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding linguistic biases.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate embeddings in middle layers decode to English versions of the correct next token, even when the input and output are non-English.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space (high entropy, no language), concept space (low entropy, English dominates), and output space (target language dominates).
The concept space is biased towards English, indicating an internal pivot language.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The token energy metric shows that latent embeddings have low energy in middle layers and high energy in later layers when the target language is selected.
papers.limitation:
Focus on the Llama-2 family limits generalizability to other models.
Tasks are simple and provide a highly controlled, toy-like context.
Limited understanding of the structure of the concept space in its original high-dimensional form.
The logit lens only grants approximate access to internal beliefs about output; other information remains hidden.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias changes when decreasing the dominance of English during training, e.g., by using different language mixtures or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks, including more culturally sensitive problems and popular use-cases.
Better understand and map out the concept space in its high-dimensional form.
papers.abstract: We ask whether multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language -- a question of key importance for understanding how language models function and the origins of linguistic bias. Focusing on the Llama-2 family of transformer models, our study uses carefully constructed non-English prompts with a unique correct single-token continuation. From layer to layer, transformers gradually map an input embedding of the final prompt token to an output embedding from which next-token probabilities are computed. Tracking intermediate embeddings through their high-dimensional space reveals three distinct phases, whereby intermediate embeddings (1) start far away from output token embeddings; (2) already allow for decoding a semantically correct next token in the middle layers, but give higher probability to its version in English than in the input language; (3) finally move into an input-language-specific region of the embedding space. We cast these results into a conceptual model where the three phases operate in "input space", "concept space", and "output space", respectively. Crucially, our evidence suggests that the abstract "concept space" lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding the biases held by multilingual language models.

papers.title: SocioProbe: What, When, and Where Language Models Learn about Sociodemographics
papers.research_question: What, when, and where do language models learn about sociodemographics? Specifically, to what extent do they encode such knowledge, how much pre-training data is needed, where in the model is it located, does it differ in multilingual models, and what is the effect of supplementary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SocioProbe, a method to probe sociodemographic knowledge in PLMs, and finds that such knowledge is encoded but is more diffuse than lower-level linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: We find that sociodemographic knowledge is located in PLMs, but much more diffuse than lower-level aspects. We hope that our findings will fuel further research towards human-like language understanding.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs encode sociodemographic knowledge, but the extent varies across models and textual domains.
Sociodemographic knowledge requires large amounts of pre-training data and learning curves do not flatten.
Sociodemographic knowledge is less localized in model layers compared to syntactic knowledge (e.g., CoLA).
In multilingual models, the localization of sociodemographic knowledge is similar to monolingual models.
Supplementary training on intermediate tasks (STILTs) can overwrite sociodemographic knowledge in the higher layers.
papers.limitation:
Predictive methods can result in potentially harmful applications (dual use).
Gender is modeled as a binary variable, not reflecting the full spectrum of identities.
Models are limited to single-GPU, general-purpose pre-trained models; results may differ for larger or domain-specific models.
future_direction: Extend analysis to languages other than English
Explore models with different architectures and pre-training objectives
Investigate sociodemographic knowledge in larger and domain-specific models
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) have outperformed other NLP models on a wide range of tasks. Opting for a more thorough understanding of their capabilities and inner workings, researchers have established the extend to which they capture lower-level knowledge like grammaticality, and mid-level semantic knowledge like factual understanding. However, there is still little understanding of their knowledge of higher-level aspects of language. In particular, despite the importance of sociodemographic aspects in shaping our language, the questions of whether, where, and how PLMs encode these aspects, e.g., gender or age, is still unexplored. We address this research gap by probing the sociodemographic knowledge of different single-GPU PLMs on multiple English data sets via traditional classifier probing and information-theoretic minimum description length probing. Our results show that PLMs do encode these sociodemographics, and that this knowledge is sometimes spread across the layers of some of the tested PLMs. We further conduct a multilingual analysis and investigate the effect of supplementary training to further explore to what extent, where, and with what amount of pre-training data the knowledge is encoded. Our overall results indicate that sociodemographic knowledge is still a major challenge for NLP. PLMs require large amounts of pre-training data to acquire the knowledge and models that excel in general language understanding do not seem to own more knowledge about these aspects.

papers.title: Jump to Conclusions: Short-Cutting Transformers With Linear Transformations
papers.research_question: Is there a more accurate way to cast hidden representations into final representation substitutes than interpreting them as they are (identity mapping)?
papers.core_contribution: A simple method using linear transformations to cast hidden representations to final-layer substitutes, which improves interpretability and efficiency.
papers.conclusion: Linear mappings provide a simple and effective way to enhance the utilization of hidden representations for interpretability and efficiency, revealing linear structure in transformer components.
papers.key_findings:
Linear mappings (mat) consistently outperform identity mapping (id) in approximating future hidden representations and final predictions.
The method allows accurate prediction estimation from early layers, showing that models often predict the final output early.
The learned linear mappings generalize well across different model scales and data distributions.
When applied to early exiting, the method saves additional layers (e.g., 7.9% for GPT-2, 5.4% for BERT) while retaining 95% accuracy.
Attention sub-modules are the most tolerant to linear approximation compared to FFN and layer normalization.
papers.limitation:
Focuses only on linear transformations, leaving affine or non-linear transformations for future work.
Does not elucidate the reason for the linear structure observed in transformer inference.
Only considers post-hoc interpretability (analyzing trained models without changing weights).
Experiments are conducted only on English data.
future_direction: Exploring affine or non-linear transformations for casting hidden representations.
Integrating linear mappings into model training rather than only post-hoc analysis.
Breaking the computation into parallel tasks to improve efficiency.
Comparing the method with other approaches like Belrose et al. (2023).
Investigating the reasons for the linear structure in transformer components.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models create hidden representations of their inputs at every layer, but only use final-layer representations for prediction. This obscures the internal decision-making process of the model and the utility of its intermediate representations. One way to elucidate this is to cast the hidden representations as final representations, bypassing the transformer computation in-between. In this work, we suggest a simple method for such casting, using linear transformations. This approximation far exceeds the prevailing practice of inspecting hidden representations from all layers, in the space of the final layer. Moreover, in the context of language modeling, our method produces more accurate predictions from hidden layers, across various model scales, architectures, and data distributions. This allows "peeking" into intermediate representations, showing that GPT-2 and BERT often predict the final output already in early layers. We then demonstrate the practicality of our method to recent early exit strategies, showing that when aiming, for example, at retention of 95% accuracy, our approach saves additional 7.9% layers for GPT-2 and 5.4% layers for BERT. Last, we extend our method to linearly approximate sub-modules, finding that attention is most tolerant to this change. Our code and learned mappings are publicly available at https://github.com/sashayd/mat.

papers.title: The Generalization Ridge: Information Flow in Natural Language Generation
papers.research_question: In NLG, how does information evolve across layers during training, and how are different layers of the network functionally organized to support generalization versus memorization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces InfoRidge, an information-theoretic framework, and uses it to reveal a 'generalization ridge' in intermediate layers where predictive information peaks, indicating a trade-off between generalization and memorization.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal a consistent generalization ridge in intermediate layers, reflecting a fundamental trade-off between generalization and memorization as information flows deeper into the model.
papers.key_findings:
Predictive information peaks at intermediate layers (the 'generalization ridge') and then declines in final layers.
Incremental information gain is highest in intermediate layers.
Attention patterns show that intermediate layers attend to task-relevant (signal) tokens.
Residual scaling experiments show that under distribution shift, the model relies less on final layers and more on intermediate layers.
The generalization ridge phenomenon persists in multi-token generation scenarios.
