papers.conclusion: The MNMT architecture impacts gender bias accuracy, with Language-Specific encoders-decoders outperforming Shared encoder-decoder due to better gender encoding in embeddings and more diverted attention.
papers.key_findings:
Language-Specific encoders-decoders architecture exhibits less gender bias than Shared encoder-decoder when trained on the same data.
Source embeddings in the Language-Specific architecture encode more gender information than in the Shared architecture.
Attention in the Language-Specific architecture is more diverted (has higher coefficient of variation) than in the Shared architecture, which helps in mitigating gender bias.
Adding Russian to the language set increases the gender bias gap between Shared and Language-Specific architectures.
Manual analysis shows that most gender errors are due to assuming masculine occupations instead of feminine ones, with some errors having linguistic and cultural explanations.
papers.abstract:
Multilingual Neural Machine Translation architectures mainly differ in the
amount of sharing modules and parameters among languages. In this paper, and
from an algorithmic perspective, we explore if the chosen architecture, when
trained with the same data, influences the gender bias accuracy. Experiments in
four language pairs show that Language-Specific encoders-decoders exhibit less
bias than the Shared encoder-decoder architecture. Further interpretability
analysis of source embeddings and the attention shows that, in the
Language-Specific case, the embeddings encode more gender information, and its
attention is more diverted. Both behaviors help in mitigating gender bias.

papers.title: On the Origins of Linear Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why are high-level semantic concepts encoded linearly in the representation space of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the next token prediction objective and the implicit bias of gradient descent together promote linear representations of concepts, using a latent variable model.
papers.conclusion: Linear representations are a natural outcome of the training dynamics and objective in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations emerge when learning from data matching the latent variable model.
The implicit bias of gradient descent leads to linearity even without log-odds matching.
Experiments confirm linear representations in simulations and in LLaMA-2.
Independent concepts are represented orthogonally.
papers.limitation: The injectivity assumption might not hold in practice, and embedding and unembedding representations might not have perfectly matched representations.
papers.abstract: Recent works have argued that high-level semantic concepts are encoded "linearly" in the representation space of large language models. In this work, we study the origins of such linear representations. To that end, we introduce a simple latent variable model to abstract and formalize the concept dynamics of the next token prediction. We use this formalism to show that the next token prediction objective (softmax with cross-entropy) and the implicit bias of gradient descent together promote the linear representation of concepts. Experiments show that linear representations emerge when learning from data matching the latent variable model, confirming that this simple structure already suffices to yield linear representations. We additionally confirm some predictions of the theory using the LLaMA-2 large language model, giving evidence that the simplified model yields generalizable insights.

papers.title: The Truth is in There: Improving Reasoning in Language Models with Layer-Selective Rank Reduction
papers.research_question: Can selectively removing higher-order components of weight matrices in Transformer models improve performance on reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Selectively removing higher-order components of weight matrices via low-rank approximation (LASER) improves LLM performance on reasoning tasks, especially for less frequent facts, by denoising conflicting responses encoded in higher-order components.
papers.conclusion: LASER is an effective post-hoc intervention that improves reasoning by denoising weight matrices, and its success warrants further study on why higher-order components accumulate noise.
papers.key_findings:
LASER improves accuracy on various NLP benchmarks, with the largest gains on facts less frequent in training data.
Improvements are most pronounced when reducing rank in later MLP layers, while early layer reduction harms performance.
LASER increases model robustness to paraphrases of questions.
Higher-order components often encode noisy or conflicting responses (e.g., generic high-frequency words or incorrect answers of the same semantic type).
Composing LASER interventions across multiple layers yields further performance improvements.
papers.limitation:
LASER slightly increases perplexity on the training data, indicating a trade-off between task performance and language modeling fluency.
The improvements in non-text domains (e.g., reinforcement learning) are smaller and less consistent.
future_direction: Understanding why higher-order components in weight matrices accumulate noisy answers during training.
Investigating the effect of model architecture and other structural choices on the occurrence of this phenomenon.
Explaining why the phenomenon is specifically true for later layers in the MLP.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a fixture in modern machine learning. Correspondingly, significant resources are allocated towards research that aims to further advance this technology, typically resulting in models of increasing size that are trained on increasing amounts of data. This work, however, demonstrates the surprising result that it is often possible to significantly improve the performance of LLMs by selectively removing higher-order components of their weight matrices. This simple intervention, which we call LAyer-SElective Rank reduction (LASER), can be done on a model after training has completed, and requires no additional parameters or data. We show extensive experiments demonstrating the generality of this finding across language models and datasets, and provide in-depth analyses offering insights into both when LASER is effective and the mechanism by which it operates.

papers.title: Following the Whispers of Values: Unraveling Neural Mechanisms Behind Value-Oriented Behaviors in LLMs
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) possess neurons that encode social values and how these values influence their behaviors, with a focus on Chinese Social Values as a case study.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the ValueExploration framework to identify and analyze value-specific neurons in LLMs, demonstrating its efficacy through experiments on Chinese Social Values.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the ValueExploration framework can effectively identify value-specific neurons in LLMs, providing insights into the causal relationships between social values and model decision-making.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit different value alignment when tested in English versus Chinese, with models like Mistral showing higher sensitivity.
Value-specific neurons can be identified using an entropy-based method on activation differences, and deactivating these neurons reduces support for value-aligned behaviors.
Chinese activation data provides stronger signals for identifying value-specific neurons compared to English data.
Overlap patterns of value-specific neurons show correlations between certain values, such as Justice and Rule of Law, and are influenced by the input language.
The C-voice benchmark is more effective for value mechanism detection compared to existing datasets like BBQ and SafetyBench.
papers.limitation:
Experiments focus on smaller-scale models (7B and 8B parameters) and do not include larger models.
The research only begins to explore the causal impact of identified neurons on value-driven behaviors.
future_direction: Refine the method for identifying value-specific neurons.
Manipulate identified neurons to enhance model alignment with social values.
Explore the impact of model size on value alignment.
papers.abstract: Despite the impressive performance of large language models (LLMs), they can present unintended biases and harmful behaviors driven by encoded values, emphasizing the urgent need to understand the value mechanisms behind them. However, current research primarily evaluates these values through external responses with a focus on AI safety, lacking interpretability and failing to assess social values in real-world contexts. In this paper, we propose a novel framework called ValueExploration, which aims to explore the behavior-driven mechanisms of National Social Values within LLMs at the neuron level. As a case study, we focus on Chinese Social Values and first construct C-voice, a large-scale bilingual benchmark for identifying and evaluating Chinese Social Values in LLMs. By leveraging C-voice, we then identify and locate the neurons responsible for encoding these values according to activation difference. Finally, by deactivating these neurons, we analyze shifts in model behavior, uncovering the internal mechanism by which values influence LLM decision-making. Extensive experiments on four representative LLMs validate the efficacy of our framework. The benchmark and code will be available.

papers.title: VISIT: Visualizing and Interpreting the Semantic Information Flow of Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and visualize the semantic information flow inside transformer language models, particularly focusing on attention heads and memory values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a tool for visualizing the semantic information flow in transformer language models as an interactive flow graph, and provides new insights into layer norms as semantic filters and the existence of regularization neurons.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces a tool to visualize the semantic information flow in transformers using the logit lens, demonstrates its utility by revealing insights about layer norms and regularization neurons, and validates the approach by supporting other analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads' semantics can be projected via the OV circuit, and only the heads with the largest norms dominate the block's output.
Memory values with the highest attention scores capture the semantics of their corresponding attention head.
Layer normalization layers act as semantic filters, demoting function words and promoting content words in the residual stream.
Regularization neurons exist that are consistently highly activated, have high entropy, and may serve as a constant bias or regularization term.
The flow-graph visualization tool can qualitatively replicate mechanistic analyses, such as indirect object identification, and reveal internal information flow patterns.
papers.limitation:
Limited to English language models, particularly GPT models with multi-head attention, and insights might not generalize to other languages or datasets.
Projection methods and the intersection score Ik have limitations in capturing semantic connections between different tokens with the same meaning.
Pruning based on the assumption that the most activated neurons determine the final prediction might be misleading as less activated neurons could also be relevant.
The methods are not causal and do not employ interventions, so further investigation is needed to fully understand the mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply causal interventions to verify the findings.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in interpretability suggest we can project weights and hidden states of transformer-based language models (LMs) to their vocabulary, a transformation that makes them more human interpretable. In this paper, we investigate LM attention heads and memory values, the vectors the models dynamically create and recall while processing a given input. By analyzing the tokens they represent through this projection, we identify patterns in the information flow inside the attention mechanism. Based on our discoveries, we create a tool to visualize a forward pass of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs) as an interactive flow graph, with nodes representing neurons or hidden states and edges representing the interactions between them. Our visualization simplifies huge amounts of data into easy-to-read plots that can reflect the models' internal processing, uncovering the contribution of each component to the models' final prediction. Our visualization also unveils new insights about the role of layer norms as semantic filters that influence the models' output, and about neurons that are always activated during forward passes and act as regularization vectors.

papers.title: From Emergence to Control: Probing and Modulating Self-Reflection in Language Models
papers.abstract: Self-reflection -- the ability of a large language model (LLM) to revisit, evaluate, and revise its own reasoning -- has recently emerged as a powerful behavior enabled by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). While self-reflection correlates with improved reasoning accuracy, its origin and underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, {\it we first show that self-reflection is not exclusive to RLVR fine-tuned models: it already emerges, albeit rarely, in pretrained models}. To probe this latent ability, we introduce Reflection-Inducing Probing, a method that injects reflection-triggering reasoning traces from fine-tuned models into pretrained models. This intervention raises self-reflection frequency of Qwen2.5 from 0.6\% to 18.6\%, revealing a hidden capacity for reflection. Moreover, our analysis of internal representations shows that both pretrained and fine-tuned models maintain hidden states that distinctly separate self-reflective from non-reflective contexts. Leveraging this observation, {\it we then construct a self-reflection vector, a direction in activation space associated with self-reflective reasoning}. By manipulating this vector, we enable bidirectional control over the self-reflective behavior for both pretrained and fine-tuned models. Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks show that enhancing these vectors improves reasoning performance by up to 12\%, while suppressing them reduces computational cost, providing a flexible mechanism to navigate the trade-off between reasoning quality and efficiency without requiring additional training. Our findings further our understanding of self-reflection and support a growing body of work showing that understanding model internals can enable precise behavioral control.

papers.title: Endogenous Resistance to Activation Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether large language models can monitor their own internal states and resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, a phenomenon termed Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR).
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces and characterizes Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), showing that large language models can self-correct during inference when subjected to task-misaligned activation steering, and provides causal evidence for internal consistency-checking circuits.
papers.conclusion: ESR demonstrates that large language models have internal self-monitoring mechanisms that can resist activation steering, which has implications for both robustness and safety, highlighting the need to understand and control these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama-3.3-70B exhibits substantial Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families show it less frequently.
26 SAE latents are identified as off-topic detectors and causally linked to ESR; ablating them reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%.
ESR can be enhanced through meta-prompts, increasing the multi-attempt rate by 4.3× for Llama-3.3-70B.
Fine-tuning on self-correction examples can induce ESR-like behavior in smaller models, but only increases attempt frequency without improving success rate.
ESR has dual implications: it could protect against adversarial manipulation but might interfere with beneficial safety interventions.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on single-layer SAEs limits tracing of inter-layer dynamics.
Only 5 models tested, making it difficult to disentangle effects of scale, architecture, and training.
Judge-based evaluation involves subjective assessment of response quality.
future_direction: Investigate whether ESR emerges from RLHF or exists in pretrained representations.
Study how ESR responds to safety-relevant steering.
Explore whether ESR can be adversarially circumvented.
papers.abstract: Large language models can resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, sometimes recovering mid-generation to produce improved responses even when steering remains active. We term this Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR). Using sparse autoencoder (SAE) latents to steer model activations, we find that Llama-3.3-70B shows substantial ESR, while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families exhibit the phenomenon less frequently. We identify 26 SAE latents that activate differentially during off-topic content and are causally linked to ESR in Llama-3.3-70B. Zero-ablating these latents reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%, providing causal evidence for dedicated internal consistency-checking circuits. We demonstrate that ESR can be deliberately enhanced through both prompting and training: meta-prompts instructing the model to self-monitor increase the multi-attempt rate by 4x for Llama-3.3-70B, and fine-tuning on self-correction examples successfully induces ESR-like behavior in smaller models. These findings have dual implications: ESR could protect against adversarial manipulation but might also interfere with beneficial safety interventions that rely on activation steering. Understanding and controlling these resistance mechanisms is important for developing transparent and controllable AI systems. Code is available at github.com/agencyenterprise/endogenous-steering-resistance.

papers.title: Language Models Understand Us, Poorly
papers.research_question: What does it mean for language models to understand human language, and do current and future models achieve such understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that internal representations are sufficient for language understanding, critiques the Scaling Paradigm, and advocates for probing model internals to advance the science of understanding.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited understanding due to under-specified data, and scaling alone may not suffice without focusing on internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Understanding-as-representation is sufficient for language understanding, while as-reliability is necessary but not sufficient.
Current language models are limited by under-specification of meaning in their training data.
The Scaling Paradigm may be computationally infeasible for achieving human-like understanding.
Probing model internals is essential to advance the science of understanding.
Adding more modalities and human language aspects is needed for better models.
papers.limitation: The paper presents only one perspective and may not fully cover diverse fields or be ultimately correct.
future_direction: Probe model internals
Add more of human language such as intersubjective, multi-agent environments
Measure what models can learn
papers.abstract: Some claim language models understand us. Others won’t hear it. To clarify, I investigate three views of human language understanding: as-mapping, as-reliability and as-representation. I argue that while behavioral reliability is necessary for understanding, internal representations are sufficient; they climb the right hill. I review state-of-the-art language and multi-modal models: they are pragmatically challenged by under-specification of form. I question the Scaling Paradigm: limits on resources may prohibit scaled-up models from approaching understanding. Last, I describe how as-representation advances a science of understanding. We need work which probes model internals, adds more of human language, and measures what models can learn.

papers.title: Do Students Debias Like Teachers? On the Distillability of Bias Mitigation Methods
papers.research_question: To what extent can knowledge distillation transfer debiasing capabilities between models? Can knowledge distillation train less biased models compared to standard training? What internal mechanisms cause the debiasing behavior change after distillation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first large-scale study on the effect of knowledge distillation on debiasing capabilities, showing that vanilla KD often fails to preserve debiasing and can increase student bias, and proposes three strategies to improve distillability.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents the first study on the distillability of debiasing capabilities, showing vanilla KD does not consistently preserve debiasing, and proposes three solutions (data augmentation, iterative KD, initialization) that significantly improve distillability.
papers.key_findings:
The debiasing capability of a model is undermined post-KD; students become more biased than teachers.
Training a debiased model does not benefit from injecting teacher knowledge (KD does not improve generalization).
Although overall robustness may remain stable post-distillation, significant variations occur across different bias types.
The effectiveness of debiasing transfer depends on model scale similarity; similar scales lead to better transfer.
Larger teachers do not guarantee more robust students.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are mainly conducted on logit-based knowledge distillation. The effect of other knowledge distillation methods has not been explored.
The work does not explore the scenario where multiple teachers participate in the distillation process.
future_direction: Investigate self-distilled debiasing, where the student iteratively distills knowledge from itself rather than relying on a fixed teacher, and explicitly guide the student using counterfactual data augmentation during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective method for model compression and transferring knowledge between models. However, its effect on model's robustness against spurious correlations that degrade performance on out-of-distribution data remains underexplored. This study investigates the effect of knowledge distillation on the transferability of ``debiasing'' capabilities from teacher models to student models on natural language inference (NLI) and image classification tasks. Through extensive experiments, we illustrate several key findings: (i) overall the debiasing capability of a model is undermined post-KD; (ii) training a debiased model does not benefit from injecting teacher knowledge; (iii) although the overall robustness of a model may remain stable post-distillation, significant variations can occur across different types of biases; and (iv) we pin-point the internal attention pattern and circuit that causes the distinct behavior post-KD. Given the above findings, we propose three effective solutions to improve the distillability of debiasing methods: developing high quality data for augmentation, implementing iterative knowledge distillation, and initializing student models with weights obtained from teacher models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study on the effect of KD on debiasing and its interenal mechanism at scale. Our findings provide understandings on how KD works and how to design better debiasing methods.

papers.title: Linear representations in language models can change dramatically over a conversation
papers.research_question: How do linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models change over the course of a conversation?
papers.core_contribution: Linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models can change dramatically over the course of a conversation, flipping their meaning, which challenges static interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: Representational dynamics over conversations pose challenges for interpretability and safety (e.g., static probes may be misleading), but also point to new research directions for understanding contextual adaptation.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of factuality and ethics can flip over a conversation (e.g., in opposite day prompt).
These changes are content-dependent: generic information is preserved, while conversation-relevant information flips.
Changes occur across different model families and layers of the model.
Changes happen even when replaying off-policy conversations (scripts from other models).
Larger models show more dramatic representational changes.
papers.limitation: Evaluated a relatively small set of conversations due to the need to tailor question sets to each conversation.
future_direction: Understanding how models' representations change in various applications (e.g., codebases).
Developing more robust interpretability and safety methods that account for representation dynamics.
Methods to control adaptability (increase or decrease) for safety.
papers.abstract: Language model representations often contain linear directions that correspond to high-level concepts. Here, we study the dynamics of these representations: how representations evolve along these dimensions within the context of (simulated) conversations. We find that linear representations can change dramatically over a conversation; for example, information that is represented as factual at the beginning of a conversation can be represented as non-factual at the end and vice versa. These changes are content-dependent; while representations of conversation-relevant information may change, generic information is generally preserved. These changes are robust even for dimensions that disentangle factuality from more superficial response patterns, and occur across different model families and layers of the model. These representation changes do not require on-policy conversations; even replaying a conversation script written by an entirely different model can produce similar changes. However, adaptation is much weaker from simply having a sci-fi story in context that is framed more explicitly as such. We also show that steering along a representational direction can have dramatically different effects at different points in a conversation. These results are consistent with the idea that representations may evolve in response to the model playing a particular role that is cued by a conversation. Our findings may pose challenges for interpretability and steering -- in particular, they imply that it may be misleading to use static interpretations of features or directions, or probes that assume a particular range of features consistently corresponds to a particular ground-truth value. However, these types of representational dynamics also point to exciting new research directions for understanding how models adapt to context.

papers.title: Understanding Unreliability of Steering Vectors in Language Models: Geometric Predictors and the Limits of Linear Approximations
papers.research_question: What are the underlying factors in model activation patterns that contribute to the observed variability in CAA steering vector reliability across different datasets and target behaviors? Can the training process of CAA steering vectors be modified to produce more consistently reliable control over language model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The thesis demonstrates that steering vector unreliability is caused by a mismatch between the simple linear function class of CAA and the often non-linear latent target behavior representations. It identifies geometric predictors (directional agreement and separability) of steering reliability.
papers.conclusion: The reliability of CAA steering vectors is predictable from the geometry of the training activations. High directional agreement and clear separability along the difference-of-means line are key indicators of steerability.
papers.key_findings:
Higher cosine similarity (directional agreement) between training activation differences predicts more reliable steering.
Better separability of positive and negative activations along the steering direction predicts more reliable steering.
Steering vectors trained on different prompt variations are directionally distinct but perform similarly and have correlated efficacy across datasets.
Steering vector unreliability stems from the linear function class being too restrictive to approximate non-linear latent behavior representations.
Prompt types that leverage in-context learning (e.g., instructions, few-shot) lead to higher directional agreement and faster steering vector convergence.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to one model (Llama 2-7B-Chat) and one family of steering methods (CAA).
The analysis is restricted to binary classification tasks and may not generalize to more complex behaviors.
The study does not investigate the impact of model scale or architecture.
future_direction: Developing more robust steering methods that explicitly account for non-linear latent behavior representations.
Extending the analysis to more models, architectures, and a broader range of behaviors.
Investigating the impact of model scale on steering reliability.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a lightweight method for controlling language model behavior by adding a learned bias to the activations at inference time. Although effective on average, steering effect sizes vary across samples and are unreliable for many target behaviors. In my thesis, I investigate why steering reliability differs across behaviors and how it is impacted by steering vector training data. First, I find that higher cosine similarity between training activation differences predicts more reliable steering. Second, I observe that behavior datasets where positive and negative activations are better separated along the steering direction are more reliably steerable. Finally, steering vectors trained on different prompt variations are directionally distinct, yet perform similarly well and exhibit correlated efficacy across datasets. My findings suggest that steering vectors are unreliable when the latent target behavior representation is not effectively approximated by the linear steering direction. Taken together, these insights offer a practical diagnostic for steering unreliability and motivate the development of more robust steering methods that explicitly account for non-linear latent behavior representations.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: What Can We Actually Steer? A Multi-Behavior Study of Activation Control
papers.research_question: How does activation steering effectiveness vary across different behavior types, and can the nature of target behaviors predict steering success?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering effectiveness varies significantly by behavior type, with internal traits like personality and misalignment being more steerable than knowledge-dependent behaviors, and vector separation does not predict success.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering is not a universal control method but a semantic modulator effective for abstract, internal dispositions but ineffective for knowledge-heavy roleplay or precise formatting tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Steering effectiveness bifurcates between internal traits (e.g., personality, misalignment) and external knowledge (e.g., public figures), with internal traits being more steerable.
Trait expression follows an inverted-U curve with steering coefficient strength, peaking at moderate coefficients while coherence and relevance decline monotonically.
Vector separation metrics do not predict steering success, contradicting the intuition that larger activation differences yield better control.
Larger training datasets enable more aggressive steering without coherence collapse, improving steering quality despite smaller raw activation differences.
Misalignment behaviors such as hallucination and sycophancy are highly steerable, indicating potential safety risks where adversarial actors could easily amplify harmful traits.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily used Llama 3.1 8B, and steerability may scale non-linearly with model size.
Steering was restricted to Layer 15, and different behaviors might be localized at different layers.
Reliance on LLM-as-a-Judge (GPT-4.1) for evaluation introduces potential biases in scoring.
future_direction: Future work should explore whether more sophisticated vector diagnostics or non-linear relationships might better predict steerability.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require precise behavior control for safe and effective deployment across diverse applications. Activation steering offers a promising approach for LLMs' behavioral control. We focus on the question of how steering effectiveness varies across different behavior types and whether the nature of target behaviors can predict steering success. We address this through empirical analysis of activation steering across 50 behaviors that span persona archetypes, personality traits, misalignment behaviors, style cues, and impersonation of public figures. We present a set of comprehensive experiments on coefficient optimization, vector properties, and data requirements to provide comprehensive guidance for the implementation of activation steering. Our analysis demonstrates that steering effectiveness varies significantly by behavior type, with different behavioral categories exhibiting distinct response patterns to intervention strength. We find that trait expression follows an inverted-U curve with a steering coefficient strength. We also show that vector separation metrics do not predict steering success, but larger training datasets enable more aggressive steering. These findings provide empirically grounded guidance for implementing activation steering and demonstrate that steering effectiveness is heavily influenced by behavior type.

papers.title: Sycophancy Is Not One Thing: Causal Separation of Sycophantic Behaviors in LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether sycophantic behaviors (excessive agreement and flattery) in LLMs arise from a single mechanism or multiple distinct processes, specifically if sycophantic agreement, genuine agreement, and sycophantic praise are distinct and independently steerable.
papers.core_contribution: Sycophantic behaviors (agreement and praise) are encoded along distinct linear directions in model representations and can be independently steered, indicating that sycophancy is not a single construct but a family of separable behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Sycophancy should be reframed as a family of distinct behaviors with separable internal representations; evaluations and interventions must be behavior-specific rather than treating sycophancy as a single phenomenon.
papers.key_findings:
Sycophantic agreement, genuine agreement, and sycophantic praise each correspond to distinct subspaces in model representations.
These behaviors are independently steerable via activation addition along learned difference-in-means directions, demonstrating functional separability.
The same representational structure for these behaviors appears consistently across different model families and scales.
Early layers encode a generic agreement signal that conflates sycophantic and genuine agreement, which diverge into distinct directions in later layers.
Sycophantic praise is encoded orthogonally to agreement behaviors across all layers.
papers.limitation:
The study only examines three sycophancy-related behaviors (sycophantic agreement, genuine agreement, sycophantic praise), not the full spectrum of sycophantic behaviors such as emotional validation or mimicry.
External validation for praise is limited because existing naturalistic benchmarks (e.g., SycophancyEval, SYCON-Bench) primarily test agreement-based deference and lack a direct ecological benchmark for praise.
Evidence is restricted to linear analyses of the residual stream (difference-in-means, activation addition, subspace removal) and does not test nonlinear methods or interventions at other network sites.
future_direction: Test whether the same separable structure appears under nonlinear analysis methods, in attention or MLP activations, and in other model families or training regimes.
Extend the analysis to a broader range of sycophancy-related behaviors such as emotional validation, acceptance framing, and mimicry.
Develop naturalistic benchmarks that directly target praise or flattery to better validate the external validity of praise-related findings.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophantic behaviors -- such as excessive agreement with or flattery of the user -- but it is unclear whether these behaviors arise from a single mechanism or multiple distinct processes. We decompose sycophancy into sycophantic agreement and sycophantic praise, contrasting both with genuine agreement. Using difference-in-means directions, activation additions, and subspace geometry across multiple models and datasets, we show that: (1) the three behaviors are encoded along distinct linear directions in latent space; (2) each behavior can be independently amplified or suppressed without affecting the others; and (3) their representational structure is consistent across model families and scales. These results suggest that sycophantic behaviors correspond to distinct, independently steerable representations.

papers.title: Efficient and accurate steering of Large Language Models through attention-guided feature learning
papers.research_question: How can we improve the steering of Large Language Models by dynamically selecting token embeddings, using soft labels based on attention to prefix, and identifying relevant layers for steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an attention-guided steering framework that dynamically selects token embeddings based on attention to prefix, uses soft labels for concept vector extraction, and identifies relevant blocks via concept enrichment scores, substantially improving steering success over prior methods.
papers.conclusion: The attention-guided steering framework significantly improves steering performance and sheds light on the distribution of concept-specific features across LLM layers, opening avenues for efficient fine-tuning and understanding of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Dynamic token selection based on attention to prefix improves steering over fixed token selection.
Using soft labels (attention-to-prefix) instead of hard labels improves concept vector extraction and steering.
Concept enrichment scores based on attention can identify effective blocks for steering.
The framework nearly doubles the number of successfully steered concepts across model sizes and architectures.
The distribution of concept-specific features varies across layers and concepts.
future_direction: Advancing understanding of knowledge representation in LLMs
Developing computationally efficient fine-tuning algorithms for domain-specific applications
papers.abstract: Steering, or direct manipulation of internal activations to guide LLM responses toward specific semantic concepts, is emerging as a promising avenue for both understanding how semantic concepts are stored within LLMs and advancing LLM capabilities. Yet, existing steering methods are remarkably brittle, with seemingly non-steerable concepts becoming completely steerable based on subtle algorithmic choices in how concept-related features are extracted. In this work, we introduce an attention-guided steering framework that overcomes three core challenges associated with steering: (1) automatic selection of relevant token embeddings for extracting concept-related features; (2) accounting for heterogeneity of concept-related features across LLM activations; and (3) identification of layers most relevant for steering. Across a steering benchmark of 512 semantic concepts, our framework substantially improved steering over previous state-of-the-art (nearly doubling the number of successfully steered concepts) across model architectures and sizes (up to 70 billion parameter models). Furthermore, we use our framework to shed light on the distribution of concept-specific features across LLM layers. Overall, our framework opens further avenues for developing efficient, highly-scalable fine-tuning algorithms for industry-scale LLMs.

papers.title: LLM Agents Display Human Biases but Exhibit Distinct Learning Patterns
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LLMs exhibit human-like behavioral biases in Decisions from Experience tasks and how their learning patterns differ from humans.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs display human biases on aggregate but exhibit distinct learning patterns due to strong recency bias, lacking phenomena like 'surprise triggers change' and 'wavy recency effect' observed in humans.
papers.conclusion: LLMs appear human-like on aggregate in DFE tasks, but detailed analysis reveals different underlying processes due to recency bias, emphasizing the need for careful investigation when using LLMs to simulate human behavior.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs and humans both exhibit underweighting of rare events, but LLMs do so more extremely.
Both LLMs and humans show the correlation effect, but humans learn faster except for the Gemini-all model.
LLMs exhibit a strong recency bias, considering only the most recent outcomes, unlike humans who consider a larger window.
Humans robustly show the wavy recency effect and surprise triggers change, which are entirely absent in LLMs.
LLMs' choice patterns closely match the Recency Player strategy, indicating a reliance on recent feedback.
future_direction: Asking models to portray a specific persona or predict human choices in DFE tasks.
Fine-tuning LLMs to experience-related decision tasks to make patterns more comparable to humans.
Expanding the scope of research to more models and decision scenarios.
papers.abstract: We investigate the choice patterns of Large Language Models (LLMs) in the context of Decisions from Experience tasks that involve repeated choice and learning from feedback, and compare their behavior to human participants. We find that on the aggregate, LLMs appear to display behavioral biases similar to humans: both exhibit underweighting rare events and correlation effects. However, more nuanced analyses of the choice patterns reveal that this happens for very different reasons. LLMs exhibit strong recency biases, unlike humans, who appear to respond in more sophisticated ways. While these different processes may lead to similar behavior on average, choice patterns contingent on recent events differ vastly between the two groups. Specifically, phenomena such as ``surprise triggers change" and the ``wavy recency effect of rare events" are robustly observed in humans, but entirely absent in LLMs. Our findings provide insights into the limitations of using LLMs to simulate and predict humans in learning environments and highlight the need for refined analyses of their behavior when investigating whether they replicate human decision making tendencies.

papers.title: In-context Vectors: Making In Context Learning More Effective and Controllable Through Latent Space Steering
papers.research_question: How can in-context learning be made more effective and controllable through latent space steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes In-Context Vectors (ICV), an inference-only method that recasts in-context learning as latent space steering, making it more effective, controllable, and efficient than standard ICL and fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: ICV improves the effectiveness and efficiency of in-context learning, enabling LLMs to adapt to tasks without fine-tuning and combine multiple tasks through vector arithmetic.
papers.key_findings:
ICV outperforms standard in-context learning and LoRA fine-tuning on diverse tasks including language detoxification, style transfer, and role-playing.
The strength of ICV can be controlled by adjusting the scaling factor λ, allowing trade-offs between task adherence and semantic preservation.
ICV benefits from more demonstration examples, similar to ICL, but without context length constraints.
ICV is most effective when applied to all layers of the transformer, rather than individual layers.
ICV enables task arithmetic, allowing multiple tasks to be combined through vector addition and negation.
papers.limitation: ICV requires access to the model to add the in-context vector, which is easy for open-source models but may be a constraint for closed models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate emergent in-context learning capabilities, where they adapt to new tasks based on example demonstrations. However, in-context learning has seen limited effectiveness in many settings, is difficult to quantitatively control and takes up context window space. To overcome these limitations, we propose an alternative approach that recasts in-context learning as in-context vectors (ICV). Using ICV has two steps. We first use a forward pass on demonstration examples to create the in-context vector from the latent embedding of the LLM. This vector captures essential information about the intended task. On a new query, instead of adding demonstrations to the prompt, we shift the latent states of the LLM using the ICV. The ICV approach has several benefits: 1) it enables the LLM to more effectively follow the demonstration examples; 2) it's easy to control by adjusting the magnitude of the ICV; 3) it reduces the length of the prompt by removing the in-context demonstrations; 4) ICV is computationally much more efficient than fine-tuning. We demonstrate that ICV achieves better performance compared to standard in-context learning and fine-tuning on diverse tasks including safety, style transfer, role-playing and formatting. Moreover, we show that we can flexibly teach LLM to simultaneously follow different types of instructions by simple vector arithmetics on the corresponding ICVs.

papers.title: Transformers as Support Vector Machines
papers.research_question: Can we characterize the optimization landscape and implicit bias of transformers? How does the attention layer select and compose tokens when trained with gradient descent?
papers.core_contribution: Establishes a formal equivalence between the optimization geometry of self-attention and a hard-margin SVM problem, and characterizes the implicit bias of 1-layer transformers optimized with gradient descent.
papers.conclusion: The findings inspire a new perspective, interpreting multilayer transformers as a hierarchy of SVMs that separates and selects optimal tokens.
papers.key_findings:
Optimizing the attention layer parameterized by (K, Q) with vanishing regularization converges in direction to an SVM solution minimizing the nuclear norm of W=KQ⊤, while direct W-parameterization minimizes a Frobenius norm SVM objective.
Gradient descent for W-parameterization converges directionally to a locally-optimal solution of the attention SVM under suitable geometric conditions, and over-parameterization catalyzes global convergence.
Over-parameterization ensures feasibility of the SVM problem and guarantees a benign optimization landscape devoid of stationary points.
A generalized SVM equivalence predicts the implicit bias of 1-layer transformers with nonlinear heads/MLPs, decoupling attention weights into directional and finite components.
Numerical experiments validate the max-margin equivalence and implicit bias for general datasets.
papers.limitation: The theory applies primarily to linear prediction heads, with a generalization proposed for nonlinear heads.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multilayer transformers and deeper architectures.
Investigating the generalization dynamics of transformers based on the SVM perspective.
Exploring connections to other optimization and margin maximization problems in deep learning.
papers.abstract: Since its inception in "Attention Is All You Need", transformer architecture has led to revolutionary advancements in NLP. The attention layer within the transformer admits a sequence of input tokens $X$ and makes them interact through pairwise similarities computed as softmax$(XQK^\top X^\top)$, where $(K,Q)$ are the trainable key-query parameters. In this work, we establish a formal equivalence between the optimization geometry of self-attention and a hard-margin SVM problem that separates optimal input tokens from non-optimal tokens using linear constraints on the outer-products of token pairs. This formalism allows us to characterize the implicit bias of 1-layer transformers optimized with gradient descent: (1) Optimizing the attention layer with vanishing regularization, parameterized by $(K,Q)$, converges in direction to an SVM solution minimizing the nuclear norm of the combined parameter $W=KQ^\top$. Instead, directly parameterizing by $W$ minimizes a Frobenius norm objective. We characterize this convergence, highlighting that it can occur toward locally-optimal directions rather than global ones. (2) Complementing this, we prove the local/global directional convergence of gradient descent under suitable geometric conditions. Importantly, we show that over-parameterization catalyzes global convergence by ensuring the feasibility of the SVM problem and by guaranteeing a benign optimization landscape devoid of stationary points. (3) While our theory applies primarily to linear prediction heads, we propose a more general SVM equivalence that predicts the implicit bias with nonlinear heads. Our findings are applicable to arbitrary datasets and their validity is verified via experiments. We also introduce several open problems and research directions. We believe these findings inspire the interpretation of transformers as a hierarchy of SVMs that separates and selects optimal tokens.

papers.title: Emergent Specialization: Rare Token Neurons in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop internal mechanisms specialized for processing rare tokens during pre-training, and what are the mechanisms for their emergence and behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies rare token neurons in language models and shows they emerge through a three-phase structure during training, with coordinated activation and heavy-tailed weight distributions, suggesting a statistical mechanical basis for emergent specialization.
papers.conclusion: Language models spontaneously develop functionally specialized subnetworks for rare token processing, characterized by a three-phase structure and heavy-tailed weight distributions, suggesting emergent specialization analogous to biological complementary learning systems.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs develop dedicated 'rare token neurons' that disproportionately impact the prediction of infrequent tokens.
These specialized neurons emerge through distinct phase transitions during training, evolving from a homogeneous initial state to a functionally differentiated architecture.
The emergence of specialized neuron groups correlates with the development of heavy-tailed weight distributions.
Rare token neurons form a coordinated subnetwork that selectively co-activates while avoiding co-activation with other neurons.
Neuron influence exhibits a three-phase structure: an influential plateau, a power-law decay phase, and a rapid decay phase.
papers.limitation:
Focus on final MLP layer only, while rare token processing likely involves distributed mechanisms across multiple architectural components.
Reliance on ablation-based proxies to quantify neuron contributions, which lack the theoretical rigor of more principled attribution methods.
Constrained to next-token prediction in autoregressive language modeling, so generalizability to downstream applications is unclear.
future_direction: Examining attention heads, intermediate layers, and cross-layer interactions to provide a more comprehensive understanding of rare token processing mechanisms.
Developing precise theoretical frameworks for measuring neuron-level effects to strengthen mechanistic interpretations.
Investigating rare token processing mechanisms in downstream applications such as question-answering and mathematical reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models struggle with representing and generating rare tokens despite their importance in specialized domains. In this study, we identify neuron structures with exceptionally strong influence on language model's prediction of rare tokens, termed as rare token neurons, and investigate the mechanism for their emergence and behavior. These neurons exhibit a characteristic three-phase organization (plateau, power-law, and rapid decay) that emerges dynamically during training, evolving from a homogeneous initial state to a functionally differentiated architecture. In the activation space, rare token neurons form a coordinated subnetwork that selectively co-activates while avoiding co-activation with other neurons. This functional specialization potentially correlates with the development of heavy-tailed weight distributions, suggesting a statistical mechanical basis for emergent specialization.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Persuade? Linear Probes Can Uncover Persuasion Dynamics in Multi-Turn Conversations
papers.research_question: How do LLMs persuade in multi-turn conversations? The paper investigates using linear probes to uncover persuasion dynamics, including persuasion success, persuadee personality, and persuasion strategy.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for analyzing persuasion dynamics in LLM-driven conversations using linear probes, demonstrating that these lightweight probes can efficiently capture key aspects of persuasion (outcome, strategy, personality) and match or outperform prompting-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Linear probes are a promising, efficient tool for studying complex behaviors like persuasion in multi-turn LLM conversations, enabling fine-grained analysis at scale and offering insights into persuasion dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can accurately identify where persuasion success or failure occurs in a conversation, detect rhetorical strategies, and estimate persuadee personality.
Probes are computationally much more efficient than prompting-based methods, especially for fine-grained, multi-turn analysis.
Persuasive cues concentrate around the middle turns in human-human dialogues but shift to the final turns in synthetic LLM-generated dialogues.
Probe outputs reveal correlations between personality traits (e.g., extraversion) and the effectiveness of different rhetorical strategies.
Probes can perform as well as or even outperform prompting in some settings, such as uncovering persuasion strategy.
future_direction: Applying the probing approach to study other complex behaviours such as deception and manipulation.
Scaling the approach to larger models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have started to demonstrate the ability to persuade humans, yet our understanding of how this dynamic transpires is limited. Recent work has used linear probes, lightweight tools for analyzing model representations, to study various LLM skills such as the ability to model user sentiment and political perspective. Motivated by this, we apply probes to study persuasion dynamics in natural, multi-turn conversations. We leverage insights from cognitive science to train probes on distinct aspects of persuasion: persuasion success, persuadee personality, and persuasion strategy. Despite their simplicity, we show that they capture various aspects of persuasion at both the sample and dataset levels. For instance, probes can identify the point in a conversation where the persuadee was persuaded or where persuasive success generally occurs across the entire dataset. We also show that in addition to being faster than expensive prompting-based approaches, probes can do just as well and even outperform prompting in some settings, such as when uncovering persuasion strategy. This suggests probes as a plausible avenue for studying other complex behaviours such as deception and manipulation, especially in multi-turn settings and large-scale dataset analysis where prompting-based methods would be computationally inefficient.

papers.title: Dichotomy of Early and Late Phase Implicit Biases Can Provably Induce Grokking
papers.research_question: How can the grokking phenomenon be rigorously explained and proven in neural networks? Specifically, can it be induced by a dichotomy of early and late phase implicit biases?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that grokking arises from a dichotomy of early and late phase implicit biases in homogeneous neural nets trained with large initialization and small weight decay, providing theoretical and empirical evidence.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that grokking can be induced by the dichotomy of implicit biases and provides a theoretical framework for understanding it.
papers.key_findings:
Grokking can be rigorously proven in neural networks with large initialization and small weight decay.
The sharp transition in grokking is due to a dichotomy: early phase implicit bias towards kernel predictors and late phase bias towards min-norm/max-margin predictors.
This dichotomy leads to a sharp transition at time proportional to (1/λ) log α.
Examples in linear classification and matrix completion demonstrate grokking and a new phenomenon called 'misgrokking'.
The theory explains the effects of initialization scale and weight decay on grokking.
papers.limitation:
Assumes C2-smoothness of the model, excluding non-smooth activations like ReLU (though ReLU is used in experiments, the theory assumes smoothness for gradient flow analysis).
Focuses on homogeneous neural nets and binary classification/regression with squared loss, limiting generality.
papers.abstract: Recent work by Power et al. (2022) highlighted a surprising "grokking" phenomenon in learning arithmetic tasks: a neural net first "memorizes" the training set, resulting in perfect training accuracy but near-random test accuracy, and after training for sufficiently longer, it suddenly transitions to perfect test accuracy. This paper studies the grokking phenomenon in theoretical setups and shows that it can be induced by a dichotomy of early and late phase implicit biases. Specifically, when training homogeneous neural nets with large initialization and small weight decay on both classification and regression tasks, we prove that the training process gets trapped at a solution corresponding to a kernel predictor for a long time, and then a very sharp transition to min-norm/max-margin predictors occurs, leading to a dramatic change in test accuracy.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning is Subgraph Search: A New Lens on Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how fine-tuning works from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, viewing fine-tuning as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within the model's computational graph.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tuning, a fine-tuning method that dynamically localizes and optimizes subgraphs (circuits) within a model's computational graph, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and balancing task performance with general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Circuit-tuning provides a new method for studying learning dynamics from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, offering insights into how fine-tuning works and enabling more precise fine-tuning that balances task performance and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit-tuning provides better training stability and preserves language modeling ability better than full fine-tuning.
The functionality of specific attention heads (Subject Attribute Heads) can reverse during fine-tuning to adapt to new tasks.
Some attention heads (Subject Identification Heads) preserve their functions and are shared before and after fine-tuning.
Nodes within a circuit cooperate through division of labor and indirect interactions to complete tasks.
Edges in the computational graph exhibit strengthening and weakening akin to Hebbian learning during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The study of mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer a model to explain its behaviors. While recent studies have focused on the static mechanism of a certain behavior, the learning dynamics inside a model remain to be explored. In this work, we develop a fine-tuning method for analyzing the mechanism behind learning. Inspired by the concept of intrinsic dimension, we view a model as a computational graph with redundancy for a specific task, and treat the fine-tuning process as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within this graph. Based on this hypothesis, we propose circuit-tuning, an algorithm that iteratively builds the subgraph for a specific task and updates the relevant parameters in a heuristic way. We first validate our hypothesis through a carefully designed experiment and provide a detailed analysis of the learning dynamics during fine-tuning. Subsequently, we conduct experiments on more complex tasks, demonstrating that circuit-tuning could strike a balance between the performance on the target task and the general capabilities. Our work offers a new analytical method for the dynamics of fine-tuning, provides new findings on the mechanisms behind the training process, and inspires the design of superior algorithms for the training of neural networks.

papers.title: Transformers Are Born Biased: Structural Inductive Biases at Random Initialization and Their Practical Consequences
papers.research_question: Do randomly initialized transformers exhibit systematic structural biases, and what are their mechanisms and practical consequences?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers exhibit strong structural biases at random initialization due to representation contraction driven by MLP and attention, which persist through training and enable seed-specific fingerprinting (SeedPrint) and explain the attention-sink phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are not blank slates; they possess inherent structural biases at initialization that persist through training, with implications for model fingerprinting and architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
Randomly initialized transformers show extreme token preferences, with certain tokens predicted orders of magnitude more often than others.
This preference arises from inter-sequence representation contraction, where last-token representations from different sequences become highly similar.
The contraction is primarily driven by asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP layers, and amplified by self-attention through intra-sequence aggregation.
These initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable model identity that can be used for fingerprinting (SeedPrint).
The attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction leads to a positional discrepancy that causally explains the attention-sink phenomenon in trained LLMs.
future_direction: Design architectures that are more neutral or explicitly incorporate desired inductive biases.
Treat initialization choices as hyperparameters tuned for final model behavior, not just optimization stability.
Extend the fingerprinting method to more challenging scenarios, such as detecting obfuscated or distilled models.
papers.abstract: Transformers underpin modern large language models (LLMs) and are commonly assumed to be behaviorally unstructured at random initialization, with all meaningful preferences emerging only through large-scale training. We challenge this assumption by showing that randomly initialized transformers already exhibit strong and systematic structural biases. In particular, untrained models display extreme token preferences: across random input sequences, certain tokens are predicted with probabilities orders of magnitude larger. We provide a mechanistic explanation for this phenomenon by dissecting the transformer architecture at initialization. We show that extreme token preference arises from a contraction of token representations along a random seed-dependent direction. This contraction is driven by two interacting forces: (i) asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP sublayers induce global (inter-sequence) representation concentration, and (ii) self-attention further amplifies this effect through local (intra-sequence) aggregation. Together, these mechanisms align hidden representations along a direction determined solely by the random initialization, producing highly non-uniform next-token predictions. Beyond mechanistic insight, we demonstrate that these initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable and intrinsic model identity. Leveraging this property, we introduce SeedPrint, a fingerprinting method that can reliably distinguish models that differ only in their random initialization, even after extensive training and under substantial distribution shift. Finally, we identify a fundamental positional discrepancy inherent to the attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction that is causally linked to the attention-sink phenomenon. This discovery provides a principled explanation for the emergence of sinks and offers a pathway for their control.

papers.title: Abstraction Induces the Brain Alignment of Language and Speech Models
papers.research_question: Why do intermediate hidden states of language and speech models predict brain responses? Is this due to shared meaning abstraction rather than next-word prediction properties?
papers.core_contribution: The correspondence between speech/language models and the brain derives from shared meaning abstraction, not next-word prediction. The intrinsic dimension of representations peaks in intermediate layers and strongly predicts brain encoding performance.
papers.conclusion: Meaning abstraction, as captured by high intrinsic dimension, is the key driver of model-brain similarity, and prediction objectives alone are insufficient for achieving this alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Layerwise surprisal does not account for layerwise encoding performance, ruling out next-token predictivity as the primary driver.
Intrinsic dimension (Id) peaks in intermediate layers and tracks the construction of higher-order linguistic features (semantic abstraction).
Layerwise Id strongly correlates with layerwise brain encoding performance across models and imaging modalities.
Id and encoding performance grow in tandem over model pre-training, indicating the relationship emerges from learning.
Finetuning models to better predict brain activity causally increases both the Id and semantic content of their representations.
papers.limitation:
High intrinsic dimension is necessary but not sufficient for high neural predictivity, as demonstrated by random Fourier features.
The relationship between Id and encoding performance is weaker for some speech models (e.g., WavLM-base-plus) where low-level acoustic similarity may dominate.
future_direction: Developing better methods for extracting task-relevant structure from naturalistic data to advance encoding models.
Further investigation of linear dimensionality measures in relation to abstraction and encoding performance.
papers.abstract: Research has repeatedly demonstrated that intermediate hidden states extracted from large language models and speech audio models predict measured brain response to natural language stimuli. Yet, very little is known about the representation properties that enable this high prediction performance. Why is it the intermediate layers, and not the output layers, that are most effective for this unique and highly general transfer task? We give evidence that the correspondence between speech and language models and the brain derives from shared meaning abstraction and not their next-word prediction properties. In particular, models construct higher-order linguistic features in their middle layers, cued by a peak in the layerwise intrinsic dimension, a measure of feature complexity. We show that a layer's intrinsic dimension strongly predicts how well it explains fMRI and ECoG signals; that the relation between intrinsic dimension and brain predictivity arises over model pre-training; and finetuning models to better predict the brain causally increases both representations' intrinsic dimension and their semantic content. Results suggest that semantic richness, high intrinsic dimension, and brain predictivity mirror each other, and that the key driver of model-brain similarity is rich meaning abstraction of the inputs, where language modeling is a task sufficiently complex (but perhaps not the only) to require it.

papers.title: HACK: Hallucinations Along Certainty and Knowledge Axes
papers.research_question: How can hallucinations in large language models be categorized based on the model's internal properties (knowledge and certainty) rather than external properties, and how can this categorization inform targeted mitigation strategies?
